Real-life example: Report pipeline: Clean lines, drop empties, find max sale, zip headers — each tool explained separately with input → output.
1) map — transform every item
Calls a function on each value. Here str.strip removes spaces. map is lazy, so wrap with list(...). Empty '' stays — strip only cleans spaces, it does not drop items.
# INPUT
lines = ["  A  ", "", "  B  "]
cleaned = list(map(str.strip, lines))
# OUTPUT (same line as each print)

cleaned → ['A', '', 'B']
2) filter — keep only items that pass a test
Think of a bouncer at a door: walk through a list, and keep only the items where your test says True. Skip the rest.
# INPUT
def is_even(n):
    return n % 2 == 0   # True for 2, 4, 6...

nums = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]
evens = list(filter(is_even, nums))
# OUTPUT (same line as each print)




evens → [2, 4, 6]
2b) Same idea — keep fever temperatures
The test can be any rule. Here: keep only readings above 100.
# INPUT
def has_fever(temp):
    return temp > 100

temps = [98.6, 99.1, 101.2, 100.5]
fever = list(filter(has_fever, temps))
# OUTPUT (same line as each print)




fever → [101.2, 100.5]
StepWhat happens
1Take one item from the list
2Run your test function → True or False
3True → keep it; False → skip it
Rule: filter(test_function, items) — not every item changes; only matching items are kept.
3) max(sales, key=…) — pick the best dict
sales is the list max walks through. Whole dicts cannot usefully be compared with >, so you need key=. lambda r: r["amount"] means: for each dict r, use its amount. max compares 50000 vs 800 and returns the original dict (not just the number).
# INPUT
sales = [
    {"item": "Laptop", "amount": 50000},
    {"item": "Mouse", "amount": 800},
]
top = max(sales, key=lambda r: r["amount"])
# OUTPUT (same line as each print)




top → {'item': 'Laptop', 'amount': 50000}
4) dict(zip(...)) — headers + row → record
zip pairs by position (1st with 1st, 2nd with 2nd; stops at shortest). dict turns those (key, value) pairs into a dictionary (common CSV-style pattern).
# INPUT
headers = ["name", "qty"]
row = ["Pen", "12"]
pairs = list(zip(headers, row))
record = dict(zip(headers, row))
# OUTPUT (same line as each print)



pairs  → [('name', 'Pen'), ('qty', '12')]
record → {'name': 'Pen', 'qty': '12'}
5) zip(*rows) — unpack rows into columns
* opens the list so zip gets each row as its own argument. That turns rows into columns (handy for averages per field).
# INPUT
readings = [
    (120, 80, 98.6),
    (115, 75, 99.1),
]
sys_list, dia_list, temps = zip(*readings)
# OUTPUT (same line as each print)




sys_list → (120, 115)
dia_list → (80, 75)
temps    → (98.6, 99.1)
zip(*readings) == zip(row1, row2)
ToolJobOutput here
mapTransform every item['A', '', 'B']
filterKeep items that pass a test[2, 4, 6] or fever temps
max(..., key=…)Best item by a field{'item': 'Laptop', 'amount': 50000}
dict(zip(...))Headers + row → record{'name': 'Pen', 'qty': '12'}
zip(*rows)Rows → columns(120, 115), (80, 75), …
Step-by-step (beginner friendly)
  • Step 1 — map, filter & reduce
    map applies a function to every item. filter keeps truthy results. reduce folds a sequence (from functools).
    nums = [1, 2, 3, 4]
list(map(lambda x: x * 2, nums))     # [2, 4, 6, 8]
list(filter(lambda x: x % 2 == 0, nums))  # [2, 4]

from functools import reduce
reduce(lambda a, b: a + b, nums)   # 10
  • Step 2 — zip & enumerate
    zip pairs items from multiple sequences. enumerate adds an index.
    names = ["Anu", "Ravi"]
scores = [90, 85]
list(zip(names, scores))
# [("Anu", 90), ("Ravi", 85)]

for i, name in enumerate(names, start=1):
    print(i, name)
  • Step 3 — type, id & isinstance
    type(x) returns the exact class. id(x) returns memory address. Prefer isinstance for type checks.
    x = 42
type(x)              # <class 'int'>
id(x)                # unique object id
isinstance(x, int)   # True
isinstance(True, int)  # True — bool is subclass of int
  • Step 4 — range, len, sorted & reversed
    Common sequence utilities — know which mutate vs return new objects.
    FunctionReturnsMutates?
    len(x)countNo
    sorted(x)new listNo
    reversed(x)iteratorNo
    list.sort()NoneYes
    len([10, 20, 30])           # 3
sorted([3, 1, 2])             # [1, 2, 3]
list(reversed("abc"))         # ['c', 'b', 'a']
  • Step 5 — max & min
    max() and min() find the largest and smallest item — with optional key= for custom ordering.
    prices = [120, 45, 89, 200]
max(prices)                 # 200
min(prices)                 # 45

scores = {"Anu": 90, "Ravi": 85}
max(scores, key=scores.get)  # "Anu" (highest score)
min(scores, key=scores.get)  # "Ravi"

max([], default=0)           # 0 — empty safe


Python keywords — deeper look


filter() = keep only items that pass your test. "
        "Think of a bouncer: True means keep, False means skip. "
        "Use a small def for the test — easier than None or strip.


sorted() = returns new sorted list; original unchanged.
.sort() = sorts list in place; returns None.
Trap: x = lst.sort() makes x None.


enumerate() = gives (index, value) pairs — avoid manual range(len()).
zip() = pair items from two sequences together.


isinstance() = type check that respects inheritance — prefer over type(x) == int.


max() / min() = largest / smallest item.
On dict: compares keys by default — use key=dict.get for values.
Empty: max(items, default=0) avoids ValueError.

These builtins are classic higher-order functions (FP): they take other functions as arguments — see Functional Programming Paradigm.

Common mistakes


❌ Mistake 1 — assigning .sort() to a variable.sort() modifies the list in-place and always returns None. Assigning it to a variable silently discards the list.
❌ Bug
nums = [3, 1, 2]
x = nums.sort()
print(x)       # None  ← lost!
✔ Fix
nums = [3, 1, 2]
x = sorted(nums)
print(x)       # [1, 2, 3]
💡 Use sorted() to get a new sorted list as a value. Use .sort() only when you want to mutate in-place and don't need the result.


❌ Mistake 2 — forgetting list() around map() / filter()map() and filter() return lazy iterators, not lists. Printing them shows an object address, not the values.
❌ Bug
nums = [1, 2, 3]
result = map(lambda x: x*2, nums)
print(result)
# <map object at 0x1f3a>
✔ Fix
nums = [1, 2, 3]
result = list(map(lambda x: x*2, nums))
print(result)
# [2, 4, 6]
💡 Wrap with list() to materialise the iterator, or use a comprehension: [x*2 for x in nums]. Same applies to filter(), zip(), and reversed().


❌ Mistake 3 — calling max() / min() on an empty sequenceIf the iterable is empty, max() and min() raise a ValueError with no default protection.
❌ Bug
scores = []
best = max(scores)
# ValueError: max() arg is
# an empty sequence
✔ Fix
scores = []
best = max(scores, default=0)
print(best)    # 0  (safe)

# or guard:
if scores:
    best = max(scores)
💡 The default= keyword (Python 3.4+) lets max() / min() return a fallback value instead of crashing.


❌ Mistake 4 — type(x) == int instead of isinstance()type() does an exact match — it ignores inheritance. Since bool is a subclass of int, type(True) == int returns False.
❌ Bug
def is_number(x):
    return type(x) == int

print(is_number(42))    # True
print(is_number(True))  # False ← wrong!
✔ Fix
def is_number(x):
    return isinstance(x, int)

print(is_number(42))    # True
print(is_number(True))  # True  ✔
💡 isinstance() respects the class hierarchy. It also accepts a tuple: isinstance(x, (int, float)) to check multiple types at once.


Before → After (Pythonic)



  
❌ Non-Pythonic
result = []
for item in items:
    result.append(item * 2)

idx = 0
for name in names:
    print(idx, name)
    idx += 1

x = my_list.sort()   # x is None!

  
→

  
✔ Pythonic
result = [item * 2 for item in items]
# or: list(map(lambda x: x*2, items))

for idx, name in enumerate(names):
    print(idx, name)

x = sorted(my_list)  # x is the list




Self-check quiz



  
Q1. What does x = my_list.sort() put in x?
    
Show answer
      
None — .sort() mutates in place and returns nothing. Use sorted(my_list) to capture the sorted result in a variable.

    

  

  
Q2. max({"a": 3, "b": 7}) — what does it return and why?
    
Show answer
      
"b" — iterating a dict yields its keys, so max compares alphabetically. To find the key with the highest value: max(d, key=d.get).

    

  

  
Q3. isinstance(True, int) — True or False? Why?
    
Show answer
      
True — bool is a subclass of int. type(True) == int is False (exact match only).

    

  

  
Q4. How many pairs does list(zip([1,2,3], ["a","b"])) produce?
    
Show answer
      
2 — zip() stops at the shortest iterable. The third element is silently dropped.

    

  

  
Q5. list(enumerate(["x","y"], start=1)) — result?
    
Show answer
      
[(1, 'x'), (2, 'y')] — start= sets the initial counter.

    

  

  
Q6. list(filter(None, [0, 1, False, 2, '', 'hi'])) — what is kept?
    
Show answer
      
[1, 2, 'hi'] — None as function keeps only truthy values.

    

  

  
Q7. sorted('python') — what type and what content?
    
Show answer
      
A list: ['h','n','o','p','t','y'] — sorted() works on any iterable and returns a new list.

    

  

  
Q8. list(map(len, ['hi','hello','hey'])) — result?
    
Show answer
      
[2, 5, 3] — map() applies len to each string.

    

  

  
Q9. max([3,1,4], key=lambda x: -x) — result?
    
Show answer
      
1 — negated values are [-3,-1,-4]; max of those is -1, corresponding to original 1.

    

  

  
Q10. list(zip(*[[1,2],[3,4],[5,6]])) — what does * do?
    
Show answer
      
[(1,3,5),(2,4,6)] — * unpacks the list so zip gets three separate args, transposing the matrix.

    

  




Interview — questions & answers
Q: sorted() vs list.sort()?
A: sorted() returns a new sorted list; original unchanged. .sort() mutates in place and returns None. Never assign x = lst.sort().
Q: When do you use enumerate?
A: When you need both index and value: for i, item in enumerate(items): instead of manual range(len(items)).
Q: isinstance vs type() == ?
A: isinstance(x, int) respects inheritance (True for bool). type(x) == int is exact match only.
Q: map vs list comprehension?
A: Comprehensions are more Pythonic and readable. map is useful with existing functions: map(str.strip, lines).
Q: max/min on empty iterable?
A: Without default=, raises ValueError. Use max(items, default=0) when empty is possible.
Q: max on a dict — what does it return?
A: By default compares keys. Use max(d, key=d.get) to find the key with the largest value.

Definition
The collections module adds specialized containers beyond plain list / dict / tuple.
  • Counting / grouping: Counter · defaultdict (auto-creates missing keys).
  • Structure: namedtuple (named fields) · deque (fast ends) · ChainMap (layered dicts).
  • Note: OrderedDict is less needed in 3.7+ (normal dict keeps insertion order).


Decision flowchart


Read from the top. If the answer is YES, stop at that box. If NO, go down.



  

    
I need a special collection helperExtra tools on top of normal list/dict

    

    
      

        
Do you need to count how many times each thing appears?

        

          

          
NO

          

            YES
            

            

              Use Counter
              Like tally marks for each word or color.
              Counter(words).most_common()
            

          

        

      

      

        
Are you sorting items into groups inside a loop?

        

          

          
NO

          

            YES
            

            

              Use defaultdict
              Empty group appears by itself when you need it — then add the item.
              defaultdict(list)groups[k].append(v)
            

          

        

      

      

        
Do you need fast add/remove at both ends (front and back)?

        

          

          
NO

          

            YES
            

            

              Use deque
              A line where people can join at the front or the back quickly.
              deque()deque(maxlen=n)
            

          

        

      

      

        
Do you want a tiny fixed record with names (x, y)?

        

          

          
NO

          

            YES
            

            

              Use namedtuple
              A tuple you can call by field name — light and clear.
              Point = namedtuple(...)Point(1, 2)
            

          

        

      

    

    

      Two layers of settings
      Look in your dict first, then a backup dict — without copying everything.
      ChainMap(Dict1, Dict2)

Key terms explained




TermMeaningQuick example


CounterCounter = dict subclass counting hashable items — one-line frequency tally. Counter("hello")


defaultdictdefaultdict = dict with factory for missing keys — no KeyError. defaultdict(list)


dequedeque = double-ended queue — fast append/pop at both ends. maxlen optional. deque() / deque(maxlen=2)


namedtuplenamedtuple = tuple with named fields — lightweight record. Point(10, 20).x


ChainMapChainMap = stack dicts — lookup tries each in order (first match wins). Does not merge copies. ChainMap(Dict1, Dict2)


OrderedDictOrderedDict = dict remembering insertion order (regular dict since 3.7). legacy code


UserDict / UserList / UserStringSubclass-friendly wrappers. Real data lives in .data.
  Override methods (e.g. __setitem__) safely — unlike subclassing built-in dict/list.
  class D(UserDict): ...


Real-life example: Support dashboard: Count statuses, group by assignee, chat buffer, light record — each collection with input → output.
1) Counter — status pie chart
Pass a list of statuses to Counter — it tallies how many times each value appears (like counting colored chips for a pie chart). Use print to see the result.
# INPUT
from collections import Counter
statuses = ["open", "open", "closed", "open"]
pie = Counter(statuses)
print(pie)
# OUTPUT (same line as each print)



Counter({'open': 3, 'closed': 1})
2) defaultdict(list) — group by assignee
Append ticket ids per person — if the key is missing, defaultdict(list) auto-creates an empty list (no KeyError, no manual if key not in dict). See Common mistakes below for without vs with comparison and the one trap.
# INPUT
from collections import defaultdict
by_assignee = defaultdict(list)
by_assignee["Ravi"].append(101)   # first touch → creates []
by_assignee["Anu"].append(102)
print(dict(by_assignee))
# OUTPUT (same line as each print)




{'Ravi': [101], 'Anu': [102]}
3) deque() first — then optional maxlen
maxlen is not required. Use plain deque() for a normal queue. Add maxlen only when you want a rolling buffer that drops the oldest item.
1) deque() — no max
# INPUT
from collections import deque
chat = deque()            # grows freely
chat.append("hi")
chat.append("ticket #42")
print(list(chat))
# OUTPUT (same line as each print)




['hi', 'ticket #42']
2) deque(maxlen=…) — rolling
# INPUT
from collections import deque
chat = deque(maxlen=2)    # keep last 2 only
chat.append("hi")
chat.append("ticket #42")
chat.append("bye")      # "hi" dropped
print(list(chat))
# OUTPUT (same line as each print)





['ticket #42', 'bye']
Rule: deque() = unlimited. deque(maxlen=n) = keep last n items only.
4) namedtuple — light ticket record
Fixed fields like a mini struct — access with t.id and t.status.
# INPUT
from collections import namedtuple
Ticket = namedtuple("Ticket", "id status")
t = Ticket(101, "open")
print(t)
# OUTPUT (same line as each print)



Ticket(id=101, status='open')

Step-by-step (beginner friendly)
  • Step 1 — Counter
    Counts hashable elements — like a frequency table.
    from collections import Counter

c = Counter("hello")
# Counter({'l': 2, 'h': 1, 'e': 1, 'o': 1})
c.most_common(2)   # [('l', 2), ('o', 1)]
c["l"]             # 2
  • Step 2 — OrderedDict
    Dict that remembers insertion order. In Python 3.7+ regular dicts also preserve order — OrderedDict adds extra methods.
    from collections import OrderedDict

od = OrderedDict()
od["a"] = 1
od["b"] = 2
print(list(od.keys()))   # ['a', 'b']
od.move_to_end("a")
print(list(od.keys()))   # ['b', 'a']
  • Step 3 — defaultdict
    Auto-creates a default value for missing keys — great for grouping tickets by assignee.
    Plain dict — set value
    by_assignee = {}
by_assignee["Ravi"].append(101)
# KeyError: "Ravi" — key does not exist yet

# Manual fix every time:
if "Ravi" not in by_assignee:
    by_assignee["Ravi"] = []
by_assignee["Ravi"].append(101)
    ✔ defaultdict(list)
    from collections import defaultdict
by_assignee = defaultdict(list)
by_assignee["Ravi"].append(101)   # OK
by_assignee["Anu"].append(102)   # OK
print(dict(by_assignee))
# {'Ravi': [101], 'Anu': [102]}
    One trap — read this slowly:
    You might write if myDict["ghost"]: meaning “only run if ghost already has tickets.”
    But Python checks the condition first. To evaluate myDict["ghost"], it must look up that key — and defaultdict creates "ghost": [] on lookup.
    The empty list is falsy, so the if body is skipped — but the unwanted key is already in the dict.
    from collections import defaultdict
myDict = defaultdict(list)
print(dict(myDict))           # {}

if myDict["ghost"]:          # lookup runs FIRST → creates []
    print("has tickets") # never runs — [] is falsy

print(dict(myDict))           # {'ghost': []}  unwanted key!

# Safe — check membership without creating:
if "ghost" in myDict:
    print(myDict["ghost"])
    from collections import defaultdict

groups = defaultdict(list)
for name, dept in [("Anu", "IT"), ("Ravi", "HR"), ("Priya", "IT")]:
    groups[dept].append(name)
print(dict(groups))
# {"IT": ["Anu", "Priya"], "HR": ["Ravi"]}
  • Step 4 — ChainMap
    Layers multiple dicts into one view. ChainMap(Dict1, Dict2) checks Dict1 first; if the key is missing, it falls through to Dict2. It does not copy or merge the dicts — it searches in order.
    # INPUT
    from collections import ChainMap

Dict1 = {"color": "blue"}                   # checked first
Dict2 = {"color": "red", "size": "M"}       # fallback
print("Dict1:", Dict1)
print("Dict2:", Dict2)

CombinedDict = ChainMap(Dict1, Dict2)  # Dict1 first, then Dict2

print(CombinedDict)           # whole ChainMap
print(CombinedDict["color"])  # blue — in Dict1
print(CombinedDict["size"])   # M — not in Dict1 → Dict2
    # OUTPUT (same line as each print)
    











    Dict1: {'color': 'blue'}
    Dict2: {'color': 'red', 'size': 'M'}
    ChainMap({'color': 'blue'}, {'color': 'red', 'size': 'M'})
    blue
    M
    Lookup order: ChainMap(Dict1, Dict2) → try Dict1, then Dict2. First match wins. Real apps: CLI args → env vars → config file defaults.
  • Step 5 — namedtuple
    Lightweight tuple with named fields — readable and immutable.
    from collections import namedtuple

Point = namedtuple("Point", ["x", "y"])
p = Point(10, 20)
p.x, p.y   # 10, 20
p[0]       # 10 (still indexable)
  • Step 6 — deque
    Double-ended queue — fast append/pop at both ends. maxlen is optional.
    1) deque() — no max
    from collections import deque

d = deque([1, 2, 3])      # grows freely
d.append(4)              # right → [1,2,3,4]
d.appendleft(0)          # left  → [0,1,2,3,4]
print(d.popleft())       # 0
print(list(d))           # [1, 2, 3, 4]
    2) deque(maxlen=…) — rolling
    from collections import deque

d = deque(maxlen=2)      # keep last 2 only
d.append("hi")
d.append("ticket #42")
d.append("bye")          # "hi" dropped
print(list(d))           # ['ticket #42', 'bye']
    Rule: deque() = unlimited. deque(maxlen=n) = keep last n only.
  • Step 7 — UserDict, UserList & UserString
    What they are: wrappers around a real dict / list / str stored in .data. Designed so you can subclass and override methods safely.

    Why not subclass built-in dict? Built-in dict methods are implemented in C. Some call each other without going through your Python overrides — so d["A"] = 1 might bypass your __setitem__. UserDict routes through Python methods, so your override always runs.

    Line-by-line for the example:
    from collections import UserDict

class CaseInsensitiveDict(UserDict):
    def __setitem__(self, key, value):
        # __setitem__ runs for: d[key] = value
        # key.lower() → store under one form ("Name" and "name" → "name")
        super().__setitem__(key.lower(), value)
        # super() = UserDict.__setitem__ → writes into self.data

d = CaseInsensitiveDict()
d["Name"] = "Anu"     # stored as key "name"
d["NAME"] = "Ravi"    # same slot — overwrites
print(d["name"])      # Ravi  (lookup still needs care — see tip)
print(d.data)         # {'name': 'Ravi'}  ← real dict inside
    __setitem__(self, key, value): Python calls this when you write d[key] = value.
    key.lower(): normalize the key so case does not create different slots.
    super().__setitem__(...): call the parent’s store logic (puts the pair into self.data) — do not reinvent storage.

    Same idea: UserList (wraps a list in .data), UserString (wraps a string). Override methods there the same way.
    Tip: for a full case-insensitive dict, also override __getitem__ / __contains__ to .lower() the key on read (otherwise d["Name"] after storing "name" may miss). The example above focuses on write-side normalization.


Python keywords — deeper look


defaultdict(list) = auto-creates empty list for missing keys — replaces if key not in d: d[key]=[] pattern.


namedtuple = tuple with named fields — Point(10,20).x instead of [0].
Counter = count occurrences like a frequency table.


UserDict / UserList = subclass-friendly wrappers — safer to extend than built-in dict/list directly.

Common mistakes


❌ Mistake 1 — manual counting with dict instead of CounterCounter is the Pythonic tool for frequency counting. Doing it manually is verbose and error-prone.
❌ Bug
words = ["a", "b", "a", "c", "a"]
counts = {}
for w in words:
    if w in counts:
        counts[w] += 1
    else:
        counts[w] = 0  # bug: should be 1 first time!
✔ Fix
from collections import Counter
words = ["a", "b", "a", "c", "a"]
counts = Counter(words)
print(counts)         # Counter({'a':3,'b':1,'c':1})
print(counts.most_common(2))  # top 2
💡 Counter handles missing keys automatically and provides .most_common(n), arithmetic operators, and subtraction.


❌ Mistake 2 — grouping with plain dict instead of defaultdict(list)When you .append() to a missing key, a normal dict raises KeyError. You must create the empty list yourself first — easy to forget.
Plain dict — set value
by_assignee = {}
by_assignee["Ravi"].append(101)
# KeyError: 'Ravi' — key does not exist yet

# Manual fix (verbose):
if "Ravi" not in by_assignee:
    by_assignee["Ravi"] = []
by_assignee["Ravi"].append(101)
✔ With defaultdict
from collections import defaultdict
by_assignee = defaultdict(list)
by_assignee["Ravi"].append(101)   # OK
by_assignee["Anu"].append(102)   # OK
print(dict(by_assignee))
# {'Ravi': [101], 'Anu': [102]}
💡 defaultdict(list) calls list() the first time you touch a missing key — you get [] automatically, then .append() works.


⚠ One trap — if myDict["key"]: can create a key by accidentYou might think if myDict["ghost"]: means “skip if ghost has no tickets.” Python evaluates the condition first — looking up myDict["ghost"] creates "ghost": []. The empty list is falsy (if body skipped), but the key is already in the dict.
Looks safe — adds key anyway
from collections import defaultdict
myDict = defaultdict(list)
print(dict(myDict))           # {}

if myDict["ghost"]:          # Step 1: lookup → creates "ghost": []
    print("tickets")    # Step 2: [] is falsy → skipped

print(dict(myDict))           # {"ghost": []}  surprise!
Safe check first
from collections import defaultdict
myDict = defaultdict(list)

if "ghost" in myDict:        # only asks — never creates
    print(myDict["ghost"])

myDict["Ravi"].append(101)   # OK — you mean to use this key
print(dict(myDict))          # {"Ravi": [101]}
💡 Rule: "key" in myDict = peek (safe). myDict["key"] = touch (creates missing key). Use myDict[key].append(...) only when you want that group.


❌ Mistake 3 — using list as a queue (O(n) popleft)Removing from the front of a list (list.pop(0)) shifts all elements — O(n). deque does it in O(1).
❌ Bug
queue = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
queue.pop(0)   # O(n) — shifts every element
queue.pop(0)   # slow for large queues
✔ Fix
from collections import deque
queue = deque([1, 2, 3, 4, 5])
queue.popleft()   # O(1) — fast!
queue.appendleft(0)  # O(1) prepend
💡 Use deque whenever you need efficient adds/removes from both ends. Use list for random access by index.


Before → After (Pythonic)



  
❌ Manual grouping
records = [("A",1),("B",2),("A",3)]
groups = {}
for k, v in records:
    if k not in groups:
        groups[k] = []
    groups[k].append(v)

  
→

  
✔ defaultdict
from collections import defaultdict
records = [("A",1),("B",2),("A",3)]
groups = defaultdict(list)
for k, v in records:
    groups[k].append(v)
# {'A': [1, 3], 'B': [2]}




Self-check quiz



  
Q1. Counter('aab') — result?
    
Show answer
      
Counter({'a': 2, 'b': 1}) — counts each character in the string.

    

  

  
Q2. defaultdict(int)['missing'] — what is returned?
    
Show answer
      
0 — int() is called as the factory, returning 0 for any missing key.

    

  

  
Q3. deque vs list for popleft() — which is faster?
    
Show answer
      
deque — O(1) vs O(n) for lists, because no element shifting is needed.

    

  

  
Q4. Counter({'a':2}) - Counter({'a':3}) — result?
    
Show answer
      
Counter() — Counter subtraction drops zero and negative counts.

    

  

  
Q5. namedtuple vs regular tuple?
    
Show answer
      
namedtuple has named fields (p.x, p.y) while regular tuples use only index access (p[0]).

    

  

  
Q6. ChainMap(Dict1, Dict2)['key'] — which dict is searched first?
    
Show answer
      
Dict1 — ChainMap searches maps in order, so the first mapping takes priority.

    

  

  
Q7. deque(maxlen=3) — what happens when you append a 4th item?
    
Show answer
      
The oldest item is automatically removed from the other end — a rolling window.

    

  




Interview — questions & answers
Q: When use defaultdict vs normal dict?
A: When you would write if key not in d: d[key] = [] every time — defaultdict creates the default for you.
Q: namedtuple vs dataclass?
A: namedtuple is immutable and lighter. dataclass is better when you need mutability, defaults, or methods.
Q: When use deque over list?
A: When you need fast appendleft/popleft — queues, BFS, sliding windows. List pop(0) is O(n).
Q: What is ChainMap for?
A: Layered lookup: ChainMap(Dict1, Dict2) checks Dict1 first, then Dict2. First match wins — no copy/merge.
Q: Why UserDict instead of subclassing dict?
A: Built-in dict methods are in C and may skip your Python overrides. UserDict stores items in .data and calls your __setitem__ / __getitem__ reliably — safer when customizing behavior (e.g. case-insensitive keys).

Memory Management & Garbage Collection

  
Python frees memory with reference counting plus a generational GC for circular references. Refcount…

Definition
Python frees memory with reference counting plus a generational GC for circular references.
  • Refcount: when count hits zero, the object is reclaimed immediately.
  • Cycles: A↔B need the gc module — refcount alone is not enough.
  • Tools: del removes a name · weakref · with for resource cleanup — profile before tuning GC.


Decision flowchart


Read from the top. If the answer is YES, stop at that box. If NO, go down.



  

    
Python is cleaning up memoryFree objects that nothing holds anymore

NO

          

            YES
            

            

              Reference counting
              Refcount hit 0 — no variable, dict slot, or attribute holds it. CPython frees it right away.
              del xx = Nonescope ends
            

          

        

      

      

        
Do two objects point at each other in a circle?

        

          

          
NO

          

            YES
            

            

              Generational GC
              A special cleaner finds circles that refcount alone can’t free.
              gc modulecircular refs
            

          

        

      

      

        
Do you want a soft link that does not keep the object alive?

        

          

          
NO

          

            YES
            

            

              Use weakref
              A soft look: you can peek later, but you do not keep the object alive.
              weakref.ref(obj)

Circular refs need gc (generational collector).





Who frees memory?



  

    
Reference counting

    
  • del / rebind
  • count → 0
  • freed immediately

  

  
vs

  

    
Garbage collector

    
  • Breaks cycles
  • A↔B both live
  • gc.collect()

  

  




Key terms explained 




TermMeaningQuick example


Reference countingCount how many names point to a toy. When count is 0, free it now.sys.getrefcount


Garbage collectorExtra cleaner for circles (A→B→A) that refcount cannot free alone.gc.collect()


Generation (GC)Young vs old buckets — young toys are checked more often (0, 1, 2).gen 0, 1, 2


weakrefSoft look at an object. Does not keep it alive.
  Later soft_ref() returns the object or None if it was freed. Good for caches.weakref.ref(obj)


delDrop a name (strong reference −1). If count hits 0 → free now.
  Does not always free circles (A↔B) — then GC is needed.del x


gc.collect()Run cyclic GC now (usually automatic). Frees unreachable circles
  that refcount alone cannot. Returns how many objects were collected.gc.collect()





  Why so many words? CPython uses refcount + cyclic GC + weakref together.
  C# mostly says “the GC” (+ WeakReference / using). Open C# Comparison for a term-by-term map
  and full detail on weakref.ref, del, and gc.collect().




Strong name & strong reference



  A strong reference is any normal hold that adds +1 to the object’s refcount
  (keeps the toy alive). A strong name is the usual case: a variable like a
  that points at the object. Other strong holds work the same way — dict slots, attributes, list items.
  del (or rebinding) drops that hold (−1). When the count hits 0, the object is freed now
  (unless a circle keeps counts above 0).





#ScenarioWhat is the strong hold?What del doesFreed when?



  1
  Dict
  Value stored under a key — d["ball"] = toy is a strong hold on toy.
  del d["ball"] drops that slot (−1).
  If that was the last strong hold → free now (refcount).




  2
  Attribute
  box.item = toy — the attribute is a strong hold on toy.
  del box.item (or box.item = None) drops it (−1).
  Last strong hold gone → free now.




  3
  Big object
  A variable name holds a large value — huge = load_report().
  del huge drops the name early so RAM can shrink sooner.
  If nothing else points at it → free now. No gc.collect() needed.




  4
  Circular ref
  a.other = b and b.other = a — each attribute is still a strong hold.
  del a, b drops the names, but A↔B attributes may still hold each other.
  Refcount may stay > 0 → need cyclic GC (gc.collect() or automatic).





# 1) Dict — strong hold in a slot
d = {"ball": obj}
del d["ball"]            # slot gone → obj freed if nothing else holds it

# 2) Attribute — strong hold on a field
box.item = obj
del box.item             # attribute gone → same idea

# 3) Big object — drop the name when finished
huge = load_report()     # strong name holds a large value
# ... use huge ...
del huge                 # free early (if last strong hold)

# 4) Circular ref — strong holds point at each other
a.other = b; b.other = a
del a, b                 # names gone, but circle may remain → gc.collect()



  Picture: a strong hold = hugging the toy.
  Dict key, attribute, and variable name are all hugs.
  del = let go. Soft look (weakref) = peek without hugging.




Strong reference vs weak reference



  Hug = strong reference (keeps the object alive).
  Peek = weak reference (weakref.ref — look later, do not keep it alive by itself).
  There is no special “peek with hug” API — hugging is a normal assignment like b = a.




  

    Strong ref — peek WITH hugging
    
a = Toy("ball")     # hug #1 (strong name)
b = a               # hug #2 — refcount +1
d["x"] = a          # hug #3 — also strong
box.item = a        # hug #4 — also strong

# each of these KEEPS the toy alive
del a, b
del d["x"]
del box.item        # last hug gone → toy freed now

    

      Effect: adds +1 to refcount. Object stays in memory while any strong hold remains.
    

  

  

    Weak ref — peek WITHOUT hugging
    
import weakref

a = Toy("ball")              # only strong hug
soft_ref = weakref.ref(a)    # peek — NO strong +1

print(soft_ref())            # Toy ball — still alive (because of a)
del a                        # last hug gone
print(soft_ref())            # None — soft look could not save it

    

      Effect: does not keep the object alive. Later soft_ref() → object or None.
    

  






Strong reference (hug)Weak reference (peek)



  How you make it
  b = a, d["k"] = a, box.item = a
  soft_ref = weakref.ref(a)




  Refcount
  +1 (keeps object alive)
  No strong +1




  Picture
  Hug the toy
  Peek / look without hugging




  After last strong hold is gone
  Object can be freed (refcount 0)
  soft_ref() returns None




  Typical use
  Normal everyday variables, dicts, attributes
  Caches / maps that must not pin memory forever




  C# twin
  Normal variable / field reference
  WeakReference<T>







  Is del mandatory on every variable? No.
  When a function ends, local names disappear automatically — same idea as del for those names.
  Do not sprinkle del through normal code. Use it when you need to remove a
  dict key / attribute, or free a big object early inside a long function.




  

    del optional — normal everyday code
    
def load():
    huge = load_report()   # strong name
    return process(huge)
# function ends → huge gone automatically
# no del needed

def greet(name):
    msg = f"Hi {name}"
    return msg
# msg disappears when greet returns

    

      Rule: short functions / locals that go out of scope —
      Python already drops the strong names. Skip del.
    

  

  

    del useful — when you really need it
    
# 1) Remove a dict key / attribute (real job)
del d["temp"]
del box.scratch

# 2) Free a big object EARLY in a long function
def overnight_batch(rows):
    huge = load_all(rows)   # still inside the function
    summary = summarize(huge)
    del huge                # done with data — free RAM now
    # ... more work that takes a long time ...
    return summary

    

      Rule: still in the same scope, but finished with a large value —
      or you must delete a key/attribute. Then del helps.
    

  






del optional (usual)del useful / needed



  When
  Function ends; name falls out of scope
  Remove key/attribute, or free early in a long function




  Who drops the hold?
  Python — automatically
  You — with del (or rebind / set to None)




  Everyday scripts / APIs?
  Yes — this is the default
  Only for keys, attributes, or big early cleanup




  Interview line
  del is optional. Scope end drops strong names.
  Use del for keys/attributes or to free a large object before a long function finishes.






weakref · del · gc.collect — two stories compared



  Same three tools. Different outcome depending on whether objects hold each other in a circle.





  

    A) No circle (simple case)
    
import gc, weakref

class Toy:
    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name

a = Toy("ball")
soft_ref = weakref.ref(a)   # soft look
print(soft_ref())           # Toy ball — still alive

del a                    # drop the only strong name
print(soft_ref())           # None — freed NOW by refcount

n = gc.collect()         # almost nothing left for GC
print(n)                 # often 0

    

      What happened: After del a, refcount hit 0 → object gone immediately.
      gc.collect() was not needed to free it.
    

  

  

    B) Circle A ↔ B (hard case)
    
import gc, weakref

class Node:
    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name
        self.other = None

a = Node("A")
b = Node("B")
a.other = b
b.other = a              # circle A ↔ B

soft_ref = weakref.ref(a)   # soft look
print(soft_ref())           # Node A — still alive

del a, b                 # drop strong names; circle may remain
print(soft_ref())           # may still be Node A

n = gc.collect()         # cyclic GC breaks the circle
print(n, soft_ref())        # collected count; soft_ref() → None

    

      What happened: After del, objects still pointed at each other.
      Refcount never hit 0 → need gc.collect() to free the circle.
    

  







ToolPurpose (always)A) No circleB) Circle A ↔ B



  weakref.ref(x)
  Soft look — does not keep object alive. Later soft_ref() → object or None.
  Watch the toy without holding it.
  Same — still only a soft look.




  del …
  Drop strong name(s). Refcount −1. If count hits 0 → free now.
  del a → count 0 → soft_ref() becomes None right away.
  del a, b → circle still holds them → may not free yet.




  gc.collect()
  Run cyclic GC now (usually automatic). Frees unreachable circles.
  Usually collects 0 for this toy — already gone.
  Needed to free A↔B; then soft_ref() becomes None.






  Takeaway:
  weakref = peek without hugging.
  del = let go of the name.
  gc.collect() = call the special cleaner when toys hold each other in a loop.

Real-life example: Overnight batch: Global cache grows forever — fix with cleanup / weakref / with — each pattern with input → output.
1) Problem — cache never clears
Storing every parsed JSON in a global dict makes RAM climb all night.
# INPUT
cache = {}

def process(order_id, huge_json):
    cache[order_id] = huge_json

process(1, {"lines": 5000})
process(2, {"lines": 5000})
# OUTPUT (same line as each print)






len(cache) → 2  (grows forever — memory leak risk)
2) Fix — stream file with with + yield
Read one line at a time; file closes when the block exits — no waiting for garbage collection.
# INPUT
def export_orders(path):
    with open(path, encoding="utf-8") as f:
        for line in f:
            yield line
# OUTPUT (same line as each print)



one line per ask; file closed after block — RAM stays flat
Step-by-step (beginner friendly)
  • Step 1 — Reference counting
    Every object tracks how many references point to it. When count hits zero, memory is reclaimed immediately — fast for most objects.
  • Step 2 — Garbage collector
    Circular references (A→B→A) keep refcounts > 0 forever. The gc module periodically finds and breaks these cycles.
  • Step 3 — Generations
    GC uses three generations — young objects collected often, old objects rarely. Tuning is rare; know it exists for leak debugging.
  • Step 4 — Practical tips
    del removes a name, not necessarily the object. Use with for files. Long-lived caches can cause memory growth — profile before optimizing.


Python keywords — deeper look


sys.getrefcount = approximate reference count (debugging only).
gc.collect() = force garbage collection — use when hunting circular-reference leaks.


del name removes the binding — object lives if other references exist.
with = deterministic cleanup for files/sockets (not every object).


      

When to use which — scenarios




SituationApproachWhy


Long-running worker memory growsProfile + check caches holding refsRefcount won't free if referenced


Parent/child mutual refsweakref or break cycle on deleteGC may delay collection


Debug "object still alive?"sys.getrefcount, gc.get_referrersFind unexpected references


File handle cleanupwith open(...) as fDeterministic — not GC-dependent




Python manages memory for you — but understanding references, cycles, and the GC helps debug leaks and performance issues in long-running services.




ConceptWhat happens


Reference countingEach object tracks how many names point to it; at zero, memory is freed immediately


Garbage collector (gc)Finds circular references reference counting cannot break


Generations 0/1/2Young objects collected more often — amortized cost


Immutable interningSmall ints and some strings may be shared — affects is tests


delRemoves a name binding — does not guarantee instant destruction





C# comparison: Python has no IDisposable pattern for every object — use with for files/sockets. GC is always on; you rarely call gc.collect() except when debugging leaks.




Common mistakes


❌ Mistake 1 — thinking del x immediately frees memorydel x removes the name binding, not the object. Memory is freed only when the reference count drops to zero.
❌ Bug
big_data = load_large_dataset()  # large object
del big_data
# object is NOT freed yet if other references exist
import gc; gc.collect()  # this actually runs GC
✔ Fix
# Ensure no other references exist:
big_data = load_large_dataset()
process(big_data)
del big_data   # removes last reference → freed
# OR: use a function scope so object goes out of scope
💡 To guarantee cleanup, ensure the object has no remaining references. Scoping (function, with block) is the cleanest approach.


❌ Mistake 2 — not using with for files and resourcesWithout with, a file may stay open if an exception occurs before the explicit .close().
❌ Bug
f = open("data.txt")
data = f.read()
# if exception happens here, file stays open!
f.close()
✔ Fix
with open("data.txt", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    data = f.read()
# file is closed automatically, even on exception
💡 with calls __exit__ (which closes the file) even if an exception is raised inside the block.


❌ Mistake 3 — circular references silently staying in memoryReference counting cannot break cycles. The garbage collector (gc module) handles them, but they can accumulate before collection.
❌ Bug
class Node:
    def __init__(self): self.ref = None

a = Node(); b = Node()
a.ref = b; b.ref = a   # cycle!
del a, b
# refcount never hits 0 — GC must clean up
✔ Fix
import weakref

class Node:
    def __init__(self): self.ref = None

a = Node(); b = Node()
a.ref = weakref.ref(b)  # weak ref — no cycle!
del b
print(a.ref())  # None — b was collected
💡 Use weakref.ref() for back-references (parent→child is strong, child→parent is weak) to avoid retention cycles.


Before → After (Pythonic)



  
❌ Manual file management
f = open("log.txt", "w")
try:
    f.write("step 1\n")
    f.write("step 2\n")
finally:
    f.close()   # explicit close needed

  
→

  
✔ Context manager
with open("log.txt", "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    f.write("step 1\n")
    f.write("step 2\n")
# closed automatically — even if exception raised




Self-check quiz



  
Q1. What is reference counting?
    
Show answer
      
Each Python object tracks how many names (variables, list elements, etc.) point to it. When the count reaches 0, the memory is freed immediately.

    

  

  
Q2. What defeats pure reference counting?
    
Show answer
      
Circular references — two objects that refer to each other keep each other's count above zero forever.

    

  

  
Q3. del x — does it immediately free the object's memory?
    
Show answer
      
Only if x was the last reference. Otherwise it just removes the name binding.

    

  

  
Q4. Which module provides manual GC control?
    
Show answer
      
gc — gc.collect() runs a full collection cycle. Rarely needed in normal code.

    

  

  
Q5. sys.getrefcount(x) returns?
    
Show answer
      
The number of references to the object (always at least 1 extra because the function argument is itself a reference).

    

  

  
Q6. What is a weak reference?
    
Show answer
      
A reference that does not increment the reference count — the object can be collected even if a weakref exists.

    

  




Interview — questions & answers
Q: How does Python free memory?
A: Primarily reference counting — when no names reference an object, it is freed. A generational GC handles circular references.
Q: What is a circular reference?
A: Two or more objects reference each other so refcounts never reach zero. Example: parent/child nodes pointing at each other — needs gc.collect() or weakref.
Q: del x vs x = None?
A: del x removes the name from the namespace. x = None rebinds to None but keeps the name. Neither guarantees instant destruction if other references exist.

Key terms explained 




TermMeaningQuick example


BaseModelPydantic schema base class with typed fields.class User(BaseModel):

Real-life example: Create-user API: Pydantic coerces and validates — no hand-written if-checks — each step with input → output.
1) Model — fields and validator
Declare types once. Field(ge=18) = age must be ≥ 18. @field_validator("email") = custom rule that runs on the email value before it is stored — here we normalize it to lowercase so Anu@Co.COM and anu@co.com become the same stored value.
# INPUT
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field, field_validator

class UserCreate(BaseModel):
    email: str
    age: int = Field(ge=18)   # built-in rule: age >= 18

    @field_validator("email")   # custom rule for email only
    @classmethod
    def lower_email(cls, v):
        # PURPOSE: clean / normalize the value (not reject it)
        # v = raw email from the client; return what to store
        return v.lower()
# OUTPUT (same line as each print)











(model ready — validates on model_validate)
Why @classmethod? Pydantic calls the validator on the class (no instance yet). v is the incoming field value; what you return becomes the final field value on the model.
1b) Does lower_email run automatically?
Yes. You never call lower_email(...) yourself. It runs when Pydantic validates — model_validate(...), UserCreate(...), or FastAPI parsing a JSON body. The decorator @field_validator("email") registers the method; Pydantic invokes it for you.
1c) More than one email rule
Add another method with the same @field_validator("email"). They run in definition order (top → bottom). Each receives the value returned by the previous one. To reject, raise ValueError("...").
# INPUT
class UserCreate(BaseModel):
    email: str
    age: int = Field(ge=18)

    @field_validator("email")
    @classmethod
    def must_have_at(cls, v):
        if "@" not in v:
            raise ValueError("email must contain @")
        return v

    @field_validator("email")
    @classmethod
    def lower_email(cls, v):
        return v.lower()     # runs after must_have_at

ok = UserCreate.model_validate({"email": "Anu@Co.COM", "age": 25})
print(ok.email)           # anu@co.com  (auto: both validators)

try:
    UserCreate.model_validate({"email": "bad", "age": 25})
except ValidationError as e:
    print(e.errors())      # must_have_at failed → 422 in FastAPI
# OUTPUT (same line as each print)

















anu@co.com




[{'type': 'value_error', 'loc': ('email',), ...}]
Tip: You can also put both checks in one method (reject + lowercase). Two methods are clearer when rules are separate.
2) Valid body — coercion works
String "25" becomes int 25; email is lowercased by the validator.
# INPUT
body = {"email": "Anu@Co.COM", "age": "25"}
user = UserCreate.model_validate(body)
print(user.email)
print(user.age)
print(user)                 # full model
# OUTPUT (same line as each print)


anu@co.com                  # lower_email ran → lowercased
25                          # "25" coerced to int
email='anu@co.com' age=25
3) Invalid age — why HTTP 422?
Age 15 fails Field(ge=18). Pydantic raises ValidationError before your route body runs. FastAPI catches that and returns HTTP 422 Unprocessable Entity (= “your JSON was understood, but the data breaks the rules”). This is not 400 from your own if checks — the framework does it for you.
# INPUT
from pydantic import ValidationError

bad = {"email": "x@y.com", "age": 15}
try:
    UserCreate.model_validate(bad)
    print("ok")
except ValidationError as e:
    print(e.error_count(), "error(s)")
    print(e.errors())          # which field + why
# OUTPUT (same line as each print)





1 error(s)

[{'type': 'greater_than_equal', 'loc': ('age',), ...}]
HTTP 422 Unprocessable Entity
In FastAPI API response
{"detail": [{"loc": ["body", "age"], "msg": "...", ...}]}
Takeaway: Field(ge=18) = door rule (reject under 18). @field_validator("email") = cleaning station (lowercase before save). 422 = “form filled wrong” — not a crash in your business logic.
Step-by-step (beginner friendly)
  • Step 1 — BaseModel
    Subclass BaseModel with typed fields — Pydantic validates on construction and coercion (e.g. string '25' → int 25).
  • Step 2 — Validation
    Field(ge=18) = built-in constraint (reject age < 18). @field_validator("email") = custom rule — Pydantic calls it automatically on model_validate / FastAPI body parse (you do not call it yourself). Here return v.lower() normalizes email. For more rules on the same field, add another @field_validator("email") method — they run top→bottom; raise ValueError to reject. Invalid data → ValidationError → FastAPI HTTP 422.
    user = UserCreate.model_validate(body)
print(user.email)   # anu@co.com  (lower_email ran automatically)
  • Step 3 — Serialization
    v2: model_validate(dict) in, model_dump() out. For ORM rows use model_config = {'from_attributes': True}.
  • Step 4 — FastAPI integration
    Route parameters typed as Pydantic models auto-parse JSON bodies and return 422 with structured errors — no manual validation boilerplate.

Common mistakes


❌ Mistake 1 — using deprecated .dict() in Pydantic v2Pydantic v2 replaced .dict() with .model_dump(). Using the old method emits a deprecation warning and will break in future versions.
❌ Bug
user = User(name="Anu", age=30)
data = user.dict()   # DeprecationWarning in v2
print(data)
✔ Fix
user = User(name="Anu", age=30)
data = user.model_dump()     # v2 method
json_str = user.model_dump_json()  # as JSON string
💡 Other renames: .parse_obj() → .model_validate(), .schema() → .model_json_schema().


❌ Mistake 2 — confusing required vs optional fieldsA field without a default is required. Using = None makes it optional. Forgetting this causes unexpected ValidationError.
❌ Bug
from pydantic import BaseModel

class Item(BaseModel):
    name: str
    price: float = None  # type mismatch: float but default None

Item(name="x")  # price=None — but type says float!
✔ Fix
from pydantic import BaseModel

class Item(BaseModel):
    name: str                  # required
    price: float | None = None # optional float
    tag: str | None = None     # optional
💡 For optional fields use float | None = None (or str | None = None). For required fields, declare just the type with no default.


❌ Mistake 3 — mutating a frozen Pydantic modelWith ConfigDict(frozen=True), instances are immutable. Trying to set an attribute raises a ValidationError.
❌ Bug
from pydantic import BaseModel, ConfigDict

class Config(BaseModel):
    model_config = ConfigDict(frozen=True)
    host: str

c = Config(host="localhost")
c.host = "remote"  # ValidationError!
✔ Fix
from pydantic import BaseModel, ConfigDict

class Config(BaseModel):
    model_config = ConfigDict(frozen=True)
    host: str

c = Config(host="localhost")
# Create new instance instead of mutating:
c2 = c.model_copy(update={"host": "remote"})
💡 Frozen models are useful for config objects and hash keys. Use .model_copy(update={}) to get a modified copy.


Before → After (Pythonic)



  
❌ Raw dict validation
def create_user(data: dict):
    # hope data has correct keys/types
    name = data["name"]        # KeyError risk
    age = int(data.get("age"))  # None cast risk
    return {"name": name, "age": age}

  
→

  
✔ Pydantic model
from pydantic import BaseModel

class User(BaseModel):
    name: str
    age: int

def create_user(data: dict) -> User:
    user = User.model_validate(data)  # validated
    return user
# ValidationError if name or age missing/wrong type




Self-check quiz



  
Q1. Pydantic v2 replacement for .dict()?
    
Show answer
      

        Answer: .model_dump()


        What it does: turns a validated model into a plain Python dict
        (field names → values) so you can print it, pass it to another API, or save it.


        Why the rename? In Pydantic v1 the method was .dict().
        v2 renamed export methods to start with model_ so they do not clash with
        a field that might be named dict, and to keep a clear “model API” family.


        Related:
        .model_dump_json() → JSON string (not a dict);
        old .json() → use .model_dump_json().
        Old .parse_obj() → .model_validate().
        Using .dict() in v2 still works briefly but shows a
        DeprecationWarning and will break later — always use .model_dump().
        
user = User(name="Anu", age=30)
print(user.model_dump())       # {'name': 'Anu', 'age': 30}
print(user.model_dump_json())  # '{"name":"Anu","age":30}'

      

    

  

  
Q2. How to make a Pydantic field required?
    
Show answer
      
Declare it with just a type and no default: name: str.

    

  

  
Q3. How to make a Pydantic field optional?
    
Show answer
      
name: str | None = None (or Optional[str] = None).

    

  

  
Q4. What does @field_validator('price') do?
    
Show answer
      
Runs a custom validation/transformation function when that field is set.

    

  

  
Q5. model_config = ConfigDict(frozen=True) — what does it do?
    
Show answer
      

        Answer: Makes instances immutable — you cannot change fields after creation
        (c.host = "remote" raises ValidationError.


        Without it (default): the model is mutable — you can reassign fields anytime
        (like a normal object). Useful for forms you keep editing; risky if the object is shared
        and someone changes it by mistake.


        With frozen=True: create once, then read-only. Good for config, IDs,
        API responses you must not accidentally overwrite.
        
# WITHOUT frozen — mutation allowed
class Config(BaseModel):
    host: str

c = Config(host="localhost")
c.host = "remote"      # OK — host is now "remote"
print(c.host)          # remote

# WITH frozen=True — mutation blocked
class Config(BaseModel):
    model_config = ConfigDict(frozen=True)
    host: str

c = Config(host="localhost")
c.host = "remote"      # ValidationError — instance is frozen
# Fix: make a new object instead
c2 = c.model_copy(update={"host": "remote"})

        

        
Without frozenWith frozen=True

        
Change field later?Yes — c.host = ... worksNo — raises error

        
How to “update”?Assign in placemodel_copy(update=...) → new instance

        
Typical useEditable drafts / working objectsConfig, constants, safe shared values

        

      

    

  

  
Q6. How to validate from a JSON string in Pydantic v2?
    
Show answer
      
Model.model_validate_json(json_str).

    

  

  
Q7. What is Field(...) used for?
    
Show answer
      
Provides metadata: description, gt/lt constraints, alias, default_factory, etc.

    

  




Interview — questions & answers
Q: What is Pydantic used for?
A: Runtime validation and parsing using type hints — API schemas, config loading, data pipelines. Core of FastAPI request/response models.
Q: Pydantic vs dataclasses?
A: Both turn typed fields into a class. The big difference: dataclasses store; Pydantic validates.
dataclassesPydantic BaseModel
JobBundle fields into an object (stdlib)Validate + coerce + export schemas
Type hintsHints only — age="25" stays a stringEnforced at runtime — "25" → int 25
Bad dataUsually accepted silentlyValidationError (FastAPI → HTTP 422)
ConstraintsYou write your own checksField(ge=18), @field_validator
API / JSONNot built for request bodiesBuilt for FastAPI schemas
When to useInternal/simple records inside your appAPI boundaries, config, untrusted input
dataclasses — no runtime check
from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass
class ItemDC:
    name: str
    age: int

ItemDC(name="Anu", age="25")
# OK — no check
# age is still str!
Pydantic — coerce + validate
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field

class ItemPyd(BaseModel):
    name: str
    age: int = Field(ge=18)

ItemPyd(name="Anu", age="25")
# coerces to int 25
# ItemPyd(..., age=15)
# → ValidationError
Interview line: dataclasses = structure; Pydantic = structure + validation. Prefer Pydantic at the edge of the system.
Q: What does @field_validator('email') do?
A: Runs custom logic on that field during validation. Common uses: normalize (v.lower()), strip spaces, or raise ValueError to reject bad values. It is not the same as Field(ge=18) — Field is a built-in constraint; the validator is your own rule.
Q: Why HTTP 422 on bad age?
A: Field(ge=18) fails → Pydantic raises ValidationError before the route body runs. FastAPI maps that to 422 Unprocessable Entity — the JSON was parsed, but the values break the schema rules.

Same name: class vs function vs method



  Toy("ball") looks like a function call, but Toy is normally a class
  (creates an object). If you later define a function with the same name, that name is
  shadowed — Python keeps only the last binding. A method named Toy
  inside the class does not replace the class.




  

    Class only — Toy("ball") creates an object
    
class Toy:
    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name

a = Toy("ball")     # class call → new object
print(a.name)       # ball

  

  

    Function reuses name Toy — class is hidden
    
class Toy:
    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name

def Toy(name):              # same name — shadows the class
    return f"fn:{name}"

a = Toy("ball")             # calls the FUNCTION
print(a)                    # fn:ball  (not a Toy object)

  




# Method named Toy — OK; does NOT replace the class
class Toy:
    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name

    def Toy(self):                  # unusual name, but allowed
        return "method Toy"

a = Toy("ball")                     # still creates the object
print(a.Toy())                      # method Toy

# Best practice: PascalCase for classes only
# use make_toy() for a helper — never shadow the class name




SituationWhat Toy(...) does


Only the class existsCreates a Toy object


A function later uses the name ToyCalls that function (class hidden)


Method def Toy(self)Class still works; call method with a.Toy()




Real-life example: Bank / wallet domain: Inheritance + polymorphism at month-end — each OOP idea with input → output.
1) Base Account — shared behaviour
Think of Account as the common blueprint for every bank account. Every account needs a balance, a way to add money (deposit), and a way to take money out (withdraw). We write those once in the base class so children (Savings, Checking, …) reuse them — that is inheritance.
Why month_end does nothing? Month-end rules differ by account type (savings may add interest; a plain wallet may do nothing). The base method is a safe default: pass means “no special month-end action.” Child classes override it when they need real logic. That way a loop can call a.month_end() on every account without crashing — polymorphism. Without a base month_end, a plain Account would raise AttributeError when you call it.
# INPUT
class Account:
    def __init__(self, balance):
        self.balance = balance   # shared state for all accounts

    def deposit(self, amount):    # shared: add money
        self.balance += amount

    def withdraw(self, amount):   # shared: remove money
        if amount > self.balance:
            raise ValueError("not enough balance")
        self.balance -= amount

    def month_end(self):
        pass   # default: do nothing (safe for plain accounts)

a = Account(100)
a.deposit(50)      # 100 → 150
a.withdraw(20)     # 150 → 130
a.month_end()      # still 130 — pass did nothing
print(a.balance)
# OUTPUT (same line as each print)



















130
Line by line: __init__ stores starting money. deposit / withdraw change that shared balance. month_end + pass = empty action on purpose — a hook for children.
2) SavingsAccount — override month_end
Child keeps deposit/withdraw from the parent, but replaces month-end with +4% interest.
# INPUT
class SavingsAccount(Account):
    def month_end(self):
        self.balance *= 1.04   # overrides Account.month_end (base was pass) — apply +4% interest

s = SavingsAccount(200)
s.deposit(0)       # still works — inherited from Account
s.month_end()      # updates balance; returns None (no return)
print(s.balance)   # print the balance — NOT print(s.month_end())
# OUTPUT (same line as each print)







208.0
Why not print(s.month_end())? month_end changes self.balance but has no return → returns None, so that print would show None.
3) Polymorphism — one loop, different behaviour
Call month_end() on every account; Python picks the right version (base pass vs savings interest).
# INPUT
accounts = [Account(100), SavingsAccount(200)]
for a in accounts:
    a.month_end()
    print(type(a).__name__, a.balance)   # runs twice
# OUTPUT (same line as each print)



Account 100
SavingsAccount 208.0
Step-by-step (beginner friendly)
  • Step 1 — Class, Object, __init__ & self
    A class is a blueprint. An object is an instance. __init__ initializes state; self refers to the current instance. __init__ is optional — only write it when you need starting values.
    # INPUT
    class Dog:
    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name

    def bark(self):
        return f"{self.name} says woof!"

my_dog = Dog("Rex")
print(my_dog.bark())
    # OUTPUT (same line as each print)
    







Rex says woof!
  • Step 2 — Same name: class vs function vs method
    Toy("ball") looks like a function call, but Toy is normally a class. If a function later uses the same name, the class is shadowed (Python keeps the last binding). A method named Toy does not replace the class.
    # INPUT
    class Toy:
    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name

a = Toy("ball")     # class → object
print(a.name)

def Toy(name):      # same name — hides the class
    return f"fn:{name}"

a = Toy("ball")     # now calls the FUNCTION
print(a)
    # OUTPUT (same line as each print)
    




ball





fn:ball
    # INPUT
    # Method named Toy — OK; class still works
class Toy:
    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name
    def Toy(self):
        return "method Toy"

a = Toy("ball")     # still creates object
print(a.Toy())
    # OUTPUT (same line as each print)
    







method Toy
    Best practice: PascalCase for classes only. Use make_toy() for a helper — never reuse the class name for a function.
  • Step 3 — Inheritance: single, multiple & MRO
    A child class inherits from one or more parents. MRO (Method Resolution Order) defines lookup order. Pet(Dog, Cat) looks left→right: Dog before Cat, so speak is Dog’s "woof". Only the first match runs — Cat.speak is not called afterward (unless Dog’s method uses super() to continue the chain).
    # INPUT
    class Animal:
    def speak(self): return "..."

class Dog(Animal):
    def speak(self): return "woof"

class Cat(Animal):
    def speak(self): return "meow"

class Pet(Dog, Cat):
    # multiple inheritance — Dog listed first
    # p.speak() → finds Dog.speak → STOPS (Cat.speak is NOT called)
    pass

p = Pet()
print(p.speak())                          # only Dog.speak runs
print([c.__name__ for c in Pet.__mro__])  # Cat is next, but unused here
    # OUTPUT (same line as each print)
    














woof
['Pet', 'Dog', 'Cat', 'Animal', 'object']
    Takeaway: Cat is on the MRO list, but speak lookup stopped at Dog.
  • Step 4 — Encapsulation & _ convention
    Python has no true private fields like C# private. Access is by convention and (for __) a rename trick — not a lock.
    So is encapsulation possible? Yes — you still bundle data + methods and mark internals as “don’t touch.” It is soft encapsulation (team discipline), not a compiler lock. What shows it in the code? self._balance / self.__pin (hidden state) + deposit() (the allowed way to change balance).
    • Public — normal name (balance): meant for callers to use.
    • “Private” by convention — one underscore (_balance): “internal — please don’t touch from outside.” Still fully reachable.
    • Name mangling — two underscores (__balance): Python renames it to _ClassName__balance so subclasses don’t accidentally overwrite it. Stronger against accidents — not security.
    Security means? A real private field would block outside code. In Python you can always write obj._balance or obj._BankAccount__balance if you know the mangled name. So _ / __ are for team discipline and avoiding name clashes, not for hiding secrets from attackers.
    # INPUT
    class BankAccount:
    def __init__(self, balance):
        self.owner = "Anu"           # public — OK to use
        self._balance = balance      # convention: internal
        self.__pin = "1234"         # mangled → _BankAccount__pin

    def deposit(self, amount):
        self._balance += amount     # class methods OK

a = BankAccount(100)
print(a.owner)                     # public
print(a._balance)                  # “private” — still works!
try:
    print(a.__pin)                 # mangled — AttributeError
except AttributeError as e:
    print(type(e).__name__ + ":", e)
print(a._BankAccount__pin)         # mangled name — still OK
print([k for k in a.__dict__])     # real attribute names
    # OUTPUT (same line as each print)
    









Anu
100



AttributeError: 'BankAccount' object has no attribute '__pin'
1234
['owner', '_balance', '_BankAccount__pin']
    Takeaway: _ = please don’t; __ = renamed; neither = locked. C# contrast: private is enforced by the compiler — Python’s _balance is a polite sign on an unlocked door.
  • Step 5 — Polymorphism & overriding
    Different classes share the same method shape (here: speak()). Child methods override parent methods. One function (announce) works with any object that has speak() — Python picks the right version at runtime.
    Interface keyword? Python has no interface keyword like C#. Saying “same interface” here means “same public methods” (duck typing), not a C# interface IAnimal type. Closest formal tool: abc.ABC + @abstractmethod (Step 6).
    # INPUT
    class Animal:
    def speak(self):
        return "..."          # base version

class Dog(Animal):
    def speak(self):
        return "woof"        # overrides Animal.speak

class Cat(Animal):
    def speak(self):
        return "meow"        # overrides Animal.speak

def announce(animal):
    print(animal.speak())  # same call — different result

announce(Dog())
announce(Cat())
announce(Animal())
    # OUTPUT (same line as each print)
    














woof
meow
...
    Takeaway: Same announce() — Dog / Cat / Animal each use their own speak().
  • Step 6 — Abstract classes (abc)
    Force subclasses to implement required methods using abc.ABC and @abstractmethod. You cannot create Shape() directly — only a complete child like Circle.
    # INPUT
    from abc import ABC, abstractmethod

class Shape(ABC):
    @abstractmethod
    def area(self):
        ...                 # must be implemented by child

class Circle(Shape):
    def __init__(self, r):
        self.r = r
    def area(self):
        return 3.14 * self.r ** 2

c = Circle(2)
print(c.area())

try:
    Shape()                 # incomplete — blocked
except TypeError as e:
    print(type(e).__name__ + ":", e)
    # OUTPUT (same line as each print)
    













12.56




TypeError: Can't instantiate abstract class Shape without an implementation for abstract method 'area'
    Takeaway: ABC = blueprint; child must fill in every @abstractmethod.
  • Step 7 — Dunder methods
    Double-underscore methods customize built-in behavior. 
    MethodTriggered byReal use
    __str__print(obj), str(obj)emails, admin UI, friendly logs
    __repr__repr(obj), debugger, listsSentry, logging %r, REPL
    __eq__obj == othercompare by id/value, not memory
    __len__len(obj)cart size, item count
    All four on one production-style model (Order):
    # INPUT
    class Order:
    def __init__(self, order_id, customer, items):
        self.order_id = order_id
        self.customer = customer
        self.items = items          # list of product names

    def __str__(self):               # users / email / admin
        return (
            f"Order #{self.order_id} for {self.customer} "
            f"— {len(self.items)} item(s)"
        )

    def __repr__(self):              # developers / logs / Sentry
        return (
            f"Order(order_id={self.order_id!r}, "
            f"customer={self.customer!r}, items={self.items!r})"
        )

    def __eq__(self, other):         # a == b by order_id
        if not isinstance(other, Order):
            return NotImplemented
        return self.order_id == other.order_id

    def __len__(self):               # len(order)
        return len(self.items)

o1 = Order(42, "Anu", ["pen", "notebook"])
o2 = Order(42, "Anu", ["pen"])       # same id → equal
o3 = Order(99, "Ravi", ["mug"])

print(o1)                           # __str__
print(repr(o1))                     # __repr__
print([o1])                         # list uses __repr__
print(o1 == o2, o1 == o3)           # __eq__
print(len(o1))                      # __len__
print(f"Email: {o1}")               # f-string → __str__
    # OUTPUT (same line as each print)
    





























Order #42 for Anu — 2 item(s)
Order(order_id=42, customer='Anu', items=['pen', 'notebook'])
[Order(order_id=42, customer='Anu', items=['pen', 'notebook'])]
True False
2
Email: Order #42 for Anu — 2 item(s)

Python keywords — deeper look


self = the current object instance — like C# this, but you must write it explicitly as the first parameter of instance methods.

Needs __init__? No. Any method can use self — constructor is optional.

Example:

class Greeter:                 # no __init__
    def hello(self, name):     # self still required
        return f"Hi, {name}"

g = Greeter()
print(g.hello("Anu"))          # Hi, Anu
# Python passes g as self automatically




__init__ = constructor — runs when the object is created. Not a type name — initializes self.

Mandatory? No. Skip it if the object needs no starting state. Python still creates the object; attributes can be set later.

Example:

# no __init__ — still valid
class Marker:
    def label(self):
        return "ok"

m = Marker()          # works — empty object
m.tag = "A"           # set attrs later if you want
print(m.label())      # ok

# with __init__ — set state at creation
class User:
    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name

u = User("Anu")       # __init__ runs here
print(u.name)         # Anu




__str__ = user-friendly print text. __repr__ = developer/debug representation.
Rule: print(obj) uses __str__.


MRO = Method Resolution Order — which parent class method runs in multiple inheritance.
Check: ClassName.__mro__


      

When to use which — scenarios




ScenarioUseWhy


Model real entity (User, Order, Dog)classBundle data + behavior


Shared behavior, different implementationsinheritance + overrideDog/Cat both speak()


Hide internal state, expose read-only@propertybalance getter without direct access


Mark "don't touch" internal field_underscoreConvention for protected (not enforced)


Force child to implement methodABC + @abstractmethodInterface-like contract


User-friendly print vs debug repr__str__ / __repr__print(obj) vs REPL display


Multiple inheritance diamond problemMROCheck Class.__mro__ for order





Real project: SavingsAccount.credit overrides the base — adds interest, then calls super().credit(...).
CurrentAccount keeps the plain credit but has a different interest_rate.
Same loop calling acct.credit(10) is polymorphism.
