Common mistakes


❌ Mistake 1 — forgetting self as the first method parameterEvery instance method must have self as its first parameter. Without it, calling the method raises a TypeError.
❌ Bug
class Dog:
    def bark(name):   # missing self
        print(f"{name} barks")

d = Dog()
d.bark()   # TypeError: bark() takes 1 argument but 2 given
✔ Fix — two valid styles
# A) store name on the object
class Dog:
    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name
    def bark(self):            # self first
        print(f"{self.name} barks")

d = Dog("Rex")
d.bark()                       # Rex barks

# B) also OK — pass name each call
class Dog:
    def bark(self, name):      # self first, then extra args
        print(f"{name} barks")

d = Dog()
d.bark("Rex")                  # Rex barks — name is an argument
💡 self is always first; extra parameters like name are fine after it. Style A keeps state on the object; style B passes data only when calling. self is a convention — Python passes the instance automatically.


❌ Mistake 2 — class-level mutable attribute shared by all instancesMutable class attributes (list, dict) are shared by all instances. Appending to one affects all.
❌ Bug
class Student:
    courses = []  # class-level — SHARED!
    def add(self, c): self.courses.append(c)

a = Student(); a.add("Math")
b = Student()
print(b.courses)  # ["Math"] ← b sees a's data!
✔ Fix
class Student:
    def __init__(self):
        self.courses = []  # instance-level
    def add(self, c): self.courses.append(c)

a = Student(); a.add("Math")
b = Student()
print(b.courses)  # []  ← independent
💡 Define mutable attributes in __init__ using self.attr = .... Class-level attributes are only safe for immutables (strings, ints) or shared constants.


❌ Mistake 3 — not calling super().__init__() in child classIf a child class overrides __init__ without calling super().__init__(), the parent's initialization is skipped.
❌ Bug
class Animal:
    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name

class Dog(Animal):
    def __init__(self, name, breed):
        self.breed = breed
        # forgot super().__init__(name)

d = Dog("Rex", "Lab")
print(d.name)   # AttributeError!
✔ Fix
class Dog(Animal):
    def __init__(self, name, breed):
        super().__init__(name)   # call parent init
        self.breed = breed

d = Dog("Rex", "Lab")
print(d.name)    # Rex
print(d.breed)   # Lab
💡 Always call super().__init__(...) in child __init__ unless you intentionally replace the parent's setup.


Before → After (Pythonic)



  
❌ Class attribute (shared)
class Cart:
    items = []     # shared by ALL Cart instances!

c1 = Cart()
c1.items.append("apple")

c2 = Cart()
print(c2.items)   # ["apple"] — unintended!

  
→

  
✔ Instance attribute
class Cart:
    def __init__(self):
        self.items = []   # each instance owns its list

c1 = Cart()
c1.items.append("apple")

c2 = Cart()
print(c2.items)   # []  ← correct




Self-check quiz



  
Q1. self in a method refers to?
    
Show answer
      
The instance on which the method is called. Python passes it automatically as the first argument.

    

  

  
Q2. @classmethod receives what as its first argument?
    
    
Show answer
      
cls — the class itself, not an instance. Used for alternative constructors.



Normal method@classmethod


First argself = this objectcls = the class


Called onusually an instance: p.greet()usually the class: Person.from_birth_year(...)


Purposeuse / change one object's datawork with the class (factories, shared setup)


Needs an instance first?Yes (you create p, then call)No — often used to create the instance




# INPUT
class Person:
    def __init__(self, name, age):
        self.name = name
        self.age = age

    # NORMAL METHOD — first arg is the instance
    def greet(self):
        return f"Hi, I am {self.name}, {self.age}"

    # CLASS METHOD — first arg is the class (Person)
    @classmethod
    def from_birth_year(cls, name, year):
        age = 2026 - year
        return cls(name, age)    # SAME as: return Person(name, age)

# Two ways to create the SAME kind of instance:
# A) normal constructor
# p = Person("Anu", 26)

# B) classmethod factory (computes age for you, then still calls __init__)
p = Person.from_birth_year("Anu", 2000)
# inside: cls(name, age) → Person("Anu", 26) → p IS a Person instance

print(type(p).__name__)                   # Person — yes, an instance
print(p.greet())                          # works because p is a real Person
print(p.name, p.age)
# OUTPUT (same line as each print)























Person
Hi, I am Anu, 26
Anu 26
p is an instance either way.
classmethod only changes HOW we create it (year → age), not WHAT p is.



Why not write Person("Anu", 26)? You can — both are fine.
from_birth_year is an extra door into the same class when you have a birth year instead of age.
Inside it still builds a normal instance with cls(...) / Person(...), so p.greet() works.


      

    

  

  
Q3. @staticmethod receives?
    
Show answer
      
No implicit first argument — it's a plain function namespaced inside the class.



Normal method@staticmethod


First argself = this objectNone automatic — just your parameters


Can useself.name, instance dataOnly arguments you pass (no self/cls)


Called asp.is_adult() (needs instance)Person.is_valid_age(20) or p.is_valid_age(20)


PurposeBehaviour of one objectUtility related to the class topic — no object state




# INPUT
class Person:
    def __init__(self, name, age):
        self.name = name
        self.age = age

    # NORMAL METHOD — needs the instance (self)
    def is_adult(self):
        return self.age >= 18

    # STATIC METHOD — plain function living in the class
    @staticmethod
    def is_valid_age(age):
        return 0 <= age <= 120   # no self / no cls

p = Person("Anu", 26)

print(p.is_adult())                 # uses p.age → True
print(Person.is_valid_age(26))      # call on class — OK
print(p.is_valid_age(-1))           # call on instance — also OK
print(Person.is_adult())            # TypeError — needs an instance
# OUTPUT (same line as each print)
















True
True
False

TypeError: Person.is_adult() missing 1 required positional argument: 'self'
static = helper with no object; normal = uses this object's data



Quick pick: need self.xxx? → normal method.
Need the class to build an object? → @classmethod.
Just a helper that fits the class topic? → @staticmethod.


      

    

  

  
Q4. __str__ vs __repr__ — which is for developers?
    
Show answer
      
__repr__ is for unambiguous developer representation. __str__ is for end-user readable output.



__str____repr__


AudienceHumans / UI / logs for usersDevelopers / debugger / REPL


Triggered byprint(obj), str(obj)repr(obj), interactive shell, many debuggers


GoalNice to readClear / ideally recreates the object




# INPUT
class Order:
    def __init__(self, order_id, customer, total):
        self.order_id = order_id
        self.customer = customer
        self.total = total

    def __str__(self):
        # user / email / admin UI / simple log line
        return f"Order #{self.order_id} for {self.customer} — ${self.total:.2f}"

    def __repr__(self):
        # developer / debugger / Sentry / logging %r
        return (
            f"Order(order_id={self.order_id!r}, "
            f"customer={self.customer!r}, total={self.total!r})"
        )

o = Order(42, "Anu", 99.5)

# --- __str__ paths (friendly) ---
print(o)                              # print → __str__
print(str(o))                         # explicit str
print(f"Email body: {o}")             # f-string uses __str__

# --- __repr__ paths (debug) ---
print(repr(o))                        # explicit repr
print([o])                            # list uses __repr__
print("debug: %r" % o)                # logging-style %r → __repr__
# OUTPUT (same line as each print)




















Order #42 for Anu — $99.50
Order #42 for Anu — $99.50
Email body: Order #42 for Anu — $99.50


Order(order_id=42, customer='Anu', total=99.5)
[Order(order_id=42, customer='Anu', total=99.5)]
debug: Order(order_id=42, customer='Anu', total=99.5)
__str__ → humans; __repr__ → developers / tools



Tip: If only __repr__ exists, print falls back to it.
Best practice: define both — __str__ nice, __repr__ precise.




Used in real production? Yes.
__str__ → user messages, emails, admin UI, simple logs (“Order #42 for Anu”).
__repr__ → debugging, Sentry/stack traces, logging with %r, REPL, and when lists/dicts print objects.
Teams often implement at least __repr__ on domain models (Order, User, Invoice) so logs are readable.


      

    

  

  
Q5. super().__init__() — when is it needed?
    
    
Show answer
      
When the child defines its own __init__ and still needs the
parent's initialisation (shared attributes / setup).
If the child has no __init__, the parent's runs automatically — no super() needed.



SituationNeed super().__init__?Why


Child has no __init__NoParent __init__ already runs


Child __init__ + needs parent attrsYesChild override skips parent unless you call it


Child fully replaces setup (rare)Usually still yesSkipping parent often leaves broken objects




# INPUT
class Animal:
    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name          # parent sets shared state

class DogBad(Animal):
    def __init__(self, name, breed):
        # forgot super().__init__(name)
        self.breed = breed

class Dog(Animal):
    def __init__(self, name, breed):
        super().__init__(name)   # run Animal.__init__ first
        self.breed = breed       # then child-only state

# --- without super (broken) ---
bad = DogBad("Rex", "Lab")
try:
    _ = bad.name                 # raises — no print here
except AttributeError as e:
    print(type(e).__name__ + ": no name — parent __init__ never ran")

# --- with super (correct) ---
d = Dog("Rex", "Lab")
print(d.name, d.breed)

# child with NO __init__ — parent runs alone, no super needed
class Cat(Animal):
    pass

c = Cat("Mittens")
print(c.name)
# OUTPUT (same line as each print)



















AttributeError: no name — parent __init__ never ran



Rex Lab






Mittens
Rule: override __init__? call super().__init__(...) unless you truly replace all parent setup.



C# twin: public Dog(string name, string breed) : base(name) { ... }
— : base(...) is the same idea as super().__init__(...).

Q7. What does ClassName.__mro__ show?
    
Show answer
      
The Method Resolution Order — the order Python searches base classes for methods
(left → right, then up the chain).

# INPUT
class Animal:
    def speak(self): return "..."

class Dog(Animal):
    def speak(self): return "woof"

class Cat(Animal):
    def speak(self): return "meow"

class Pet(Dog, Cat):
    pass

p = Pet()
print(p.speak())                           # first match on MRO wins
print([c.__name__ for c in Pet.__mro__])   # lookup order
# OUTPUT (same line as each print)













woof
['Pet', 'Dog', 'Cat', 'Animal', 'object']
Pet → Dog (found speak → stop). Cat is on the list but unused unless Dog uses super().

      

    

  

  
Q8. Difference between __new__ and __init__?
    
Show answer
      
__new__ creates the object (returns instance);
__init__ initialises it (sets attributes, returns nothing).
Override __new__ mainly for immutable types (e.g. tuple subclasses).



__new____init__


WhenBefore the object existsAfter object is created


JobAllocate / return instanceSet self.xxx


Returnsthe new objectNone (always)




# INPUT
class Demo:
    def __new__(cls, value):
        print("1) __new__ creates the object")
        obj = super().__new__(cls)   # actually make Demo instance
        return obj

    def __init__(self, value):
        print("2) __init__ initialises it")
        self.value = value

d = Demo(42)
print(d.value)
# OUTPUT (same line as each print)


1) __new__ creates the object




2) __init__ initialises it



42
Order is always: __new__ first, then __init__. Day-to-day code almost always only needs __init__.



When override __new__? Immutable subclasses — e.g. custom tuple —
because you must build the value during creation, not after.


      

    

  




Interview — questions & answers
Q: What is self in Python?
A: The current instance. You must pass it as the first parameter of instance methods. self.name stores data on the object — like this in C#.
Q: What if a function has the same name as a class?
A: Python keeps the last binding of that name. A function named Toy after class Toy shadows the class — Toy("ball") then calls the function, not the constructor. A method def Toy(self) does not replace the class. Best practice: never reuse the class name for a function.
Q: __str__ vs __repr__?
A: __str__ is for end users (readable). __repr__ is for developers — ideally valid code to recreate the object.
Q: What is MRO?
A: Method Resolution Order — the sequence Python searches base classes. Check with ClassName.__mro__ or help(ClassName).
Q: How does Python handle encapsulation?
A: By convention: _attr means internal. __attr name-mangles to _ClassName__attr. Not true access control — trust and documentation.

Descriptors

  
A descriptor is a helper object (think: security guard) that controls how an attribute is read , wri…

Definition
A descriptor is a helper object (think: security guard) that controls how an attribute is read, written, or deleted.
  • Why? Without it, person.age = -20 is stored. With it, Python asks the helper first and can raise ValueError.
  • Create in 2 steps: (1) helper class with __get__ / __set__ · (2) attach it — price = PositiveNumber() (stores a helper, not a number).
  • Non-data = only __get__ (write can bypass).
  • Data = __get__ + __set__ (every write goes through the guard).
  • @property is a built-in data descriptor.


Decision flowchart


Read from the top. If the answer is YES, stop at that box. If NO, go down.

              @property@x.setter

NO

              __get____set__

NO

Real-life example: Start with @property, then reuse the same rules with __get__ / __set__. Both reject negatives — like a C# property setter.
1) One field with @property
p.price reads the getter; p.price = … runs the setter. Naming convention: public name price → backing store self._price → getter def price → @price.setter (same name).
# INPUT
class Product:
    def __init__(self):
        self._price = 0

    @property
    def price(self):                 # getter
        return self._price

    @price.setter
    def price(self, value):          # setter
        if value < 0:
            raise ValueError("must be >= 0")
        self._price = value

p = Product()
p.price = 99
print(p.price)
# OUTPUT (same line as each print)














99


2) Two fields — @property vs descriptor (side by side) 
@property is per field (copy getter/setter again). A descriptor is defined once at class level, then plugged into every field that needs it.
@property × 2 (repeat code)
# INPUT
class Product:
    def __init__(self):
        self._price = 0
        self._qty = 0

    @property
    def price(self):
        return self._price
    @price.setter

        if value < 0:
            raise ValueError("must be >= 0")
        self._price = value

    @property
    def qty(self):                   # same rules again!
        return self._qty
    @qty.setter
    def qty(self, value):
        if value < 0:
            raise ValueError("must be >= 0")
        self._qty = value

p = Product()
p.price = 10
p.qty = 3
print(p.price, p.qty)
# OUTPUT (same line as each print)


























10 3
Descriptor once → many fields
# INPUT
class Positive:                     # define ONCE
    def __set_name__(self, owner, name):
        # NOT the constructor — runs AFTER class Product is created
        # owner = the CLASS (Product), name = 'price' / 'qty'
        self.name = name
    def __get__(self, obj, owner):
        # obj = instance p (or None if Product.price)
        # owner = class Product
        return obj.__dict__.get(self.name)
    def __set__(self, obj, value):
        # obj = instance p; value = what you assign
        if value < 0:
            raise ValueError("must be >= 0")
        obj.__dict__[self.name] = value

class Product:                      # plug in where needed
    price = Positive()              # class-level field
    qty = Positive()                # same helper again

class Order:
    total = Positive()              # reuse on another class!

p = Product()
p.price = 10
p.qty = 3
print(p.price, p.qty)
try:
    p.qty = -1
except ValueError as e:
    print(type(e).__name__)
# OUTPUT (same line as each print)

























10 3

objThe instance — here p (or None if you access Product.price on the class)
valueWhat you assign — p.price = 10 → value is 10

3) Remember
@property = fine for one-off fields. Need the same check on many fields/classes? Define a descriptor and attach it where needed — get/set logic lives in the helper, not copied.
Step-by-step (beginner friendly)
  • Step 1 — What is a descriptor? (security guard)
    Think of a descriptor as a security guard in front of a variable. Normally Python gives the value directly; with a descriptor it asks the helper first.
    Without descriptor:
  person.name  →  "John"

With descriptor:
  person.name
       │
       ▼
  Descriptor (helper)
       │
       ▼
  validate / calculate / return
    Definition: a helper object that controls how an attribute is read, written, or deleted.
    Why need it? Without it, person.age = -20 is stored. A descriptor can raise ValueError instead. Use for: validate, calculate, restrict, log, type-check.
  • Step 2 — Start with @property (getter + setter)
    Start here — like a C# property. @property + @age.setter creates a built-in data descriptor. Read → property.__get__; write → property.__set__.
    # INPUT
    class Student:
    def __init__(self):
        self._age = 0

    @property
    def age(self):                # __get__
        return self._age

    @age.setter
    def age(self, value):         # __set__
        if value < 0:
            raise ValueError("age cannot be negative")
        self._age = value

s = Student()
s.age = 20
print(s.age)
try:
    s.age = -5
except ValueError as e:
    print(type(e).__name__)
    # OUTPUT (same line as each print)
    















20



ValueError
    Public nameBacking storeGetterSetter
    priceself._price@property / def price@price.setter / def price
    ageself._age@property / def age@age.setter / def age
    Yes — follow the field name. Outside code uses p.price; inside, store in self._price (leading _ = “internal”). Never write self.price = … inside the setter — that calls the setter again.
    RememberMeaning
    DescriptorHelper that controls an attribute
    __get__Runs on read
    __set__Runs on write
    Non-dataRead helper only
    DataRead + write helper
    @propertyBuilt-in data descriptor
    One-line: A descriptor sits between your code and an attribute so Python can control read / write / delete.
  • Step 3 — Same idea with __get__ / __set__
    Same job as @property, but reusable. Define the helper once, then attach it at class level on every field that needs the same rules (price, qty, even another class).
    Step A — helper class (get/set logic lives here):
    # INPUT
    class PositiveNumber:
    def __get__(self, obj, owner):
        ...   # like @property getter
    def __set__(self, obj, value):
        ...   # like @property.setter
    # OUTPUT (same line as each print)
    




    Step B — plug into required fields (class-level — not inside __init__):
    # INPUT
    class Product:
    price = PositiveNumber()   # field 1
    qty = PositiveNumber()     # field 2 — same rules

class Order:
    total = PositiveNumber()   # reuse on another class

# p.price / p.qty / o.total all ask the same helper
    # OUTPUT (same line as each print)
    







    vs @property: two properties → copy getter/setter twice. Descriptor → one class, many field = PositiveNumber() lines. See the Real-life side-by-side above.
  • Step 4 — Type 1 Non-data vs Type 2 Data
    Only two types. Non-data = only __get__ (write can bypass). Data = __get__ + __set__ (guard on every write).
    No setter — how does get still work? On read (p.price), if the instance has no price in __dict__ yet, Python calls __get__ (default / compute / log). On write (p.price = -1), with no __set__, Python just does a normal store into p.__dict__['price'] — the helper is skipped. After that, reads often use the instance value and may skip __get__ too.
    Type 1 — Non-data (only __get__)
    # INPUT
    class SoftField:
    def __set_name__(self, owner, name):
        self.name = name
    def __get__(self, obj, owner):
        print("Reading via __get__...")
        return obj.__dict__.get(self.name, "empty")
    # NO __set__ — write is a normal store

class Product:
    price = SoftField()

p = Product()
print(p.price)      # no instance value yet → __get__
p.price = -1        # no __set__ → stored in __dict__
print(p.price)      # instance wins (may skip __get__)
    # OUTPUT (same line as each print)
    











Reading via __get__...
empty

-1
    Before write:  Class price→SoftField   Instance (empty)
               read → __get__ → 'empty'
After write:   Class price→SoftField   Instance price→-1
               read → instance value (descriptor bypassed)
    Type 2 — Data (__get__ + __set__)
    # INPUT
    class PositiveNumber:
    def __set_name__(self, owner, name):
        self.name = name
    def __get__(self, obj, owner):
        return obj.__dict__.get(self.name)
    def __set__(self, obj, value):
        if value < 0:
            raise ValueError("must be >= 0")
        obj.__dict__[self.name] = value

class Product:
    price = PositiveNumber()

p = Product()
p.price = 100
print(p.price)
try:
    p.price = -50     # always goes through __set__
except ValueError as e:
    print(type(e).__name__)
    # OUTPUT (same line as each print)
    














100



ValueError
    FeatureNon-dataData
    __get__YesYes
    __set__NoYes
    Controls write / validateNoYes
    Instance var can overrideYesNo
    When use non-data? When you only want to customize read (default / lazy / log), and it’s OK if a normal assignment overrides the helper afterward.
    # INPUT
    class DefaultTitle:
    def __get__(self, obj, owner):
        # only runs until someone assigns obj.title = ...
        # usual (with __set_name__ + store): return obj.__dict__.get(self.name)
        return obj.__dict__.get("title", "Untitled")

class Doc:
    title = DefaultTitle()     # non-data: no __set__

d = Doc()
print(d.title)        # __get__ → default
d.title = "Report"    # normal write — OK, no validation
print(d.title)        # instance value
    # OUTPUT (same line as each print)
    









Untitled

Report
    Real examples of non-data: plain functions on a class, @staticmethod, @classmethod — they use __get__ only, so you can still assign an instance attribute of the same name if needed. Need validation on every write? Use a data descriptor (or @property with a setter).
    Memory trick: Non-data = read helper only (write can override) · Data = read + write helper · @property with setter = data.
  • Step 5 — Why __dict__? (store without recursion)
    Every instance has __dict__ — the object’s storage bag (name → value). Descriptors must write here, or they call themselves again.
    # INPUT
    class Product:
    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name
        self.price = 99

p = Product("Pen")
print(p.__dict__)
print(p.__dict__["price"])
p.__dict__["price"] = 50
print(p.price)
    # OUTPUT (same line as each print)
    





{'name': 'Pen', 'price': 99}
99

50
    Bug — infinite recursion
    # INPUT
    def __set__(self, obj, value):
    obj.price = value   # calls __set__ again!
    # OUTPUT (same line as each print)
    

    Fix — write into __dict__
    # INPUT
    def __set__(self, obj, value):
    obj.__dict__[self.name] = value  # safe store
    # OUTPUT (same line as each print)
    

    Takeaway: guard = descriptor · cupboard storage = __dict__.


Python keywords — deeper look


@property = attribute that runs code on get/set but looks like a field.
Use when: validate on assign: @score.setter.
Looks like: obj.score = 5 — runs setter logic.


Descriptor = object with __get__ / __set__ — powers @property internally.


      

When to use which — scenarios




ScenarioUseWhy


Validate value on assignment@property setterReject negative temperature, age


Computed read-only field (area, full name)@property onlyNo setter — derived from other fields


Custom get/set/delete on attributedescriptor classAdvanced — __get__, __set__


Simple field with validation@propertyPrefer over full descriptor — less boilerplate


ORM field lazy-loading from DBdescriptorFramework-level attribute control





Custom descriptors implement __get__, __set__, __delete__ — @property is the common built-in form.




Common mistakes


❌ Mistake 1 — storing descriptor data on the descriptor instanceself.value = value stores on the descriptor (one object shared by every User) — so ages overwrite each other. Fix: store per instance with obj.__dict__[self.name] = value.
❌ Bug
class Validated:
    def __set__(self, obj, value):
        self.value = value  # stored on DESCRIPTOR — shared!
    def __get__(self, obj, cls):
        return self.value

class User:
    age = Validated()

u1 = User(); u1.age = 30
u2 = User(); u2.age = 25
print(u1.age)  # 25 ← wrong!
✔ Fix
class Validated:
    def __set_name__(self, owner, name):
        self.name = name
    def __set__(self, obj, value):
        obj.__dict__[self.name] = value  # on INSTANCE
    def __get__(self, obj, cls):
        if obj is None: return self
        return obj.__dict__.get(self.name)
💡 Always store data on obj.__dict__ using a key derived from __set_name__.


❌ Mistake 2 — __get__ not handling the class access case
Same method, two call paths:



You writeobj in __get__What to return


u.score (instance)the User objectthe stored value


User.score (class)Nonethe descriptor (self)



Bug: always using obj.__dict__ — crashes when obj is None.

Fix: if obj is None: return self before touching obj.__dict__.

❌ Bug
class Positive:
    def __set_name__(self, owner, name):
        self.name = name
    def __set__(self, obj, value):
        obj.__dict__[self.name] = value
    def __get__(self, obj, cls):
        # no guard — fails on class access
        return obj.__dict__[self.name]

class User:
    score = Positive()

u = User()
u.score = 10
print(u.score)      # 10 — OK (obj is u)
print(User.score)   # AttributeError: 'NoneType'
                    #   has no attribute '__dict__'
✔ Fix
class Positive:
    def __set_name__(self, owner, name):
        self.name = name
    def __set__(self, obj, value):
        obj.__dict__[self.name] = value
    def __get__(self, obj, cls):
        if obj is None:
            return self  # class → descriptor
        return obj.__dict__[self.name]

class User:
    score = Positive()

u = User()
u.score = 10
print(u.score)      # 10
print(User.score)   # <Positive object> — OK



What “<Positive object> — OK” means:
u.score → this user's value (10).
User.score → the descriptor helper on the class (not a number).
Returning self on class access is expected — it is not a bug; the guard stopped the crash on purpose.


💡 Always guard class access first: if obj is None: return self.


❌ Mistake 3 — using a data descriptor when a @property sufficesFor per-class validation that doesn't need reuse, @property is simpler than a full descriptor class.
❌ Bug
# Overkill for one-off validation:
class PositiveInt:
    def __set_name__(self, owner, name): ...
    def __get__(self, obj, cls): ...
    def __set__(self, obj, value): ...

class Order:
    qty = PositiveInt()
✔ Fix
# Simpler for one-off:
class Order:
    def __init__(self, qty):
        self.qty = qty

    @property
    def qty(self): return self._qty

    @qty.setter
    def qty(self, v):
        if v < 0: raise ValueError
        self._qty = v
💡 Use a descriptor class when the same validation logic is needed in many different classes. For one class, @property is cleaner.


Before → After (Pythonic)



  
❌ Repeated property boilerplate
class Product:
    @property
    def price(self): return self._price
    @price.setter
    def price(self, v):
        if v < 0: raise ValueError("negative")
        self._price = v

class Order:
    @property  # same code repeated!
    def qty(self): return self._qty
    @qty.setter
    def qty(self, v):
        if v < 0: raise ValueError("negative")
        self._qty = v

  
→

  
✔ Reusable descriptor
class NonNegative:
    def __set_name__(self, owner, name):
        self.name = name
    def __set__(self, obj, v):
        if v < 0: raise ValueError("negative")
        obj.__dict__[self.name] = v
    def __get__(self, obj, cls):
        if obj is None: return self
        return obj.__dict__.get(self.name)

class Product:
    price = NonNegative()

class Order:
    qty = NonNegative()




Self-check quiz



  
Q1. Minimum method needed for a descriptor?
    
Show answer
      
__get__ — makes it a non-data descriptor.

    

  

  
Q2. What makes a data descriptor vs non-data descriptor?
    
Show answer
      
Data descriptor implements both __get__ and __set__ (and/or __delete__). Non-data has only __get__.

    

  

  
Q3. Where should descriptor data be stored?
    
Show answer
      
On the instance via obj.__dict__[self.name], not on the descriptor itself.

    

  

  
Q4. __set_name__ is called when?
    
Show answer
      
When the class body is executed (class definition time) — automatically receives the attribute name.

    

  

  
Q5. Code after if obj is None: return self in __get__ handles what case?
    
Show answer
      
It handles class-level attribute access: MyClass.attr returns the descriptor itself.

    

  

  
Q6. property is what kind of descriptor?
    
Show answer
      

        A data descriptor.
        


        Step-by-step — what @property really is
        
    
          
  1. You write @property / @temp.setter / @temp.deleter.
    2. 
          
  2. Python builds one property object and puts it on the class
              (Celsius.temp.
    3. 
          
  3. That object is a descriptor: reading / writing / deleting
              c.temp call its __get__ / __set__ /
              __delete__.
    4. 
          
  4. Because it has __set__ (and usually __delete__),
              it is classified as a data descriptor — not non-data.
    5. 
          
  5. Even a read-only property (no setter written) still has
              __set__: assignment raises AttributeError
              instead of storing into __dict__.
    6. 
        

        Comparison
        

          
@property (data)Function / soft field (non-data)

          
Protocols__get__ + __set__ (+ __delete__)only __get__

          
Read obj.xruns getterruns __get__ (or returns stored value)

          
Write obj.x = valways runs setter / blocks writenormal store into obj.__dict__ — helper can be skipped

          
Can instance dict bypass?No — data descriptor winsYes — after assign, instance value usually wins

          
Typical usevalidated / computed attributesmethods, defaults, lazy helpers

        

        Write example — data vs non-data
        

          
@property (data) — always runs setter
          
class Product:
    def __init__(self):
        self._price = 0
    @property
    def price(self):
        return self._price
    @price.setter
    def price(self, value):
        print("setter ran")
        if value < 0:
            raise ValueError("must be >= 0")
        self._price = value

p = Product()
p.price = 10          # prints: setter ran
print(p.price)        # 10
# p.price = -1        # ValueError — cannot bypass

          
Non-data — normal store into __dict__
          
class Soft:
    def __set_name__(self, owner, name):
        self.name = name
    def __get__(self, obj, owner):
        print("get ran")
        return obj.__dict__.get(self.name, 0)
    # NO __set__

class Product:
    price = Soft()

p = Product()
print(p.price)        # get ran → 0
p.price = -1          # normal store — NO guard!
print(p.price)        # -1 (get may be skipped)
print(p.__dict__)     # {'price': -1}

        

        

          Takeaway: obj.x = v on a data descriptor
          (@property) always hits the setter / can block the write.
          On a non-data field, write is a plain
          obj.__dict__["x"] = v — validation is skipped.
        

      

    

  




Interview — questions & answers
Q: Is @property a descriptor?
A: Yes — start here. Built-in data descriptor: getter → __get__, setter → __set__.
Q: What is a descriptor in one line?
A: A helper object that sits between your code and an attribute and controls how it is read, written, or deleted.
Q: Non-data vs data descriptor?
A: Non-data has only __get__ — a normal instance write can bypass it. Data has __set__ too — every assignment goes through the helper (can validate).
Q: Why use obj.__dict__ inside __set__?
A: To store the value without calling the descriptor again. obj.price = value inside __set__ causes infinite recursion.
Q: When custom descriptor instead of @property?
A: When the same validation/access logic must be reused across many classes or fields (ORM-style columns).

Real-life example: Export 50M+ CSV rows: Stream with yield — avoid MemoryError from read().split() — each approach with input → output.
1) Without yield vs with yield — same job, different memory
Both parse rows. Left builds a full list in RAM. Right hands back one row at a time.
Without yield — list in RAM
# INPUT
def csv_reader(path):
    rows = []
    with open(path, encoding="utf-8") as f:
        for line in f:
            rows.append(line.strip().split(","))
    return rows          # ALL rows at once

data = csv_reader("big.csv")
print(len(data))
# OUTPUT (same line as each print)








50000000
then often → MemoryError on huge files
With yield — one row at a time
# INPUT
def csv_reader(path):
    with open(path, encoding="utf-8") as f:
        for line in f:
            yield line.strip().split(",")

# first row only
row = next(csv_reader("big.csv"))
print(row)                 # ['id', 'name', 'amount']

# ALL rows — one per loop (still lazy)
for row in csv_reader("big.csv"):
    print(row)             # each line, one at a time
# OUTPUT (same line as each print)







['id', 'name', 'amount']




then for-loop prints every remaining row
memory: still ONE row at a time — safe for 50M+
Does the for need next? No — for calls next() for you on each lap until the generator is done. Use next(gen) only when you want one row by hand.
Takeaway: return rows waits until the whole file is loaded. yield pauses after each row — caller decides when to ask for the next.
2) Export — without yield vs with yield
Same transform + write. Left loads all rows first. Right writes each row as it arrives.
Without yield — load all, then write

may finish… or MemoryError before any write
peak RAM ≈ whole file
With yield — write as you read
# INPUT
def export(path, out):
    with open(out, "w", encoding="utf-8") as dest:
        for row in csv_reader(path):  # yield version
            t = transform(row)
            dest.write(",".join(t) + "\n")

export("big.csv", "out.csv")

out file grows line by line
peak RAM ≈ one row — safe for 50M+
Compare: without yield you must hold the full list before writing. With yield, each for lap = one next() → transform → write → discard.

Same file. Left loads everything into RAM. Right keeps one line in memory.
Without yield — fails at scale

Why: read().split() / list(...) needs space for all rows at once. yield + for never builds that list.
Step-by-step (beginner friendly)
  • Step 1 — Lazy iterators (why generators exist)
    From Real Python: generators return a lazy iterator — loop like a list, but do not store all contents in memory. Loading a huge CSV with file.read().split() can raise MemoryError; yield one row at a time stays safe.
  • Step 2 — yield vs return + same function compared
    return ends with one result (or a full list). yield marks a generator function — it pauses and can produce many values over time.
    # WITHOUT yield — returns a complete list
def parse_lines_list(f):
    results = []
    for line in f:
        results.append(line.strip())
    return results

# WITH yield — generator: one line when asked
def parse_lines(f):
    for line in f:
        yield line.strip()

# Caller looks the same:
# for row in parse_lines(open("data.csv")):
#     print(row)
    Generator expression (short form, no yield keyword): (line for line in open(path))
  • Step 3 — Infinite sequences & pipelines
    Only generators can model infinite sequences safely (memory is finite). You can also chain generators into a pipeline without building giant intermediate lists.
    def infinite_sequence():
    n = 0
    while True:
        yield n
        n += 1

gen = infinite_sequence()
next(gen); next(gen)   # 0, then 1 — stop manually
  • Step 4 — Iterator protocol & itertools
    An iterable has __iter__ (can start a loop). An iterator has __iter__ and __next__ (gives the next value). for calls these until StopIteration.
    HasExample
    Iterable__iter__list, range, generator function result
    Iterator__iter__ + __next__what iter(list) returns; generators
    1) Full custom iterator — for uses __iter__ / __next__ for you:
    # INPUT
    class CountDown:
    def __init__(self, start):
        self.n = start

    def __iter__(self):
        return self          # I am my own iterator

    def __next__(self):
        if self.n <= 0:
            raise StopIteration
        self.n -= 1
        return self.n + 1

# for calls iter(), then next() until StopIteration
for x in CountDown(3):
    print(x)

# same idea by hand:
it = iter(CountDown(2))
print(next(it))
print(next(it))

Python keywords — deeper look


yield = pause function, return one value, resume on next call.
return = end function completely.
Generator = any function containing yield.


Iterator protocol = __iter__ + __next__ — for loops call these under the hood.
StopIteration = signal that iteration ended.

Also: Generator frame internals




Common mistakes


❌ Mistake 1 — trying to iterate a generator twiceA generator is exhausted after one full iteration. A second for loop over the same generator produces nothing.
❌ Bug
def evens(n):
    for i in range(n):
        if i % 2 == 0: yield i

gen = evens(10)
print(list(gen))  # [0, 2, 4, 6, 8]
print(list(gen))  # []  ← exhausted!
✔ Fix
def evens(n):
    for i in range(n):
        if i % 2 == 0: yield i

# Re-create if you need to iterate again:
print(list(evens(10)))
print(list(evens(10)))  # fresh generator
💡 Generators are one-pass iterators. Store the results in a list if you need to iterate multiple times.


❌ Mistake 2 — building a full list when a generator sufficesLoading a million items into a list before processing wastes memory. A generator computes items on demand.
❌ Bug
def process_all(n):
    return [heavy(i) for i in range(n)]  # builds full list

for result in process_all(1_000_000):
    use(result)
✔ Fix
def process_all(n):
    for i in range(n):
        yield heavy(i)  # one at a time

for result in process_all(1_000_000):
    use(result)   # constant memory
💡 Use generators for pipelines where intermediate results are consumed immediately. Use lists when you need random access or multiple passes.


❌ Mistake 3 — forgetting yield from for sub-generatorsTo delegate to another generator or iterable, use yield from. Manual iteration loses the send()/throw() channel.
❌ Bug
def combined(a, b):
    for item in a: yield item  # verbose
    for item in b: yield item

# Also misses send/throw/return transparency
✔ Fix
def combined(a, b):
    yield from a  # cleaner, preserves protocol
    yield from b

# yield from also works with any iterable:
yield from range(5)
💡 yield from expr is a full two-way channel: it forwards send(), throw(), and captures the sub-generator's return value.


Before → After (Pythonic)



  
❌ List-based (high memory)
def read_large_file(path):
    with open(path) as f:
        return f.readlines()   # entire file in memory!

for line in read_large_file("huge.log"):
    process(line)

  
→

  
✔ Generator (streaming)
def read_large_file(path):
    with open(path, encoding="utf-8") as f:
        for line in f:
            yield line.rstrip()  # one line at a time

for line in read_large_file("huge.log"):
    process(line)




Self-check quiz



  
Q1. What keyword makes a function a generator?
    
Show answer
      
yield — any function containing yield returns a generator object when called.

    

  

  
Q2. What does a generator raise when all values are yielded?
    
Show answer
      
StopIteration — consumed by for loops automatically.

    

  

  
Q3. Can you iterate a generator twice without re-creating it?
    
Show answer
      
No — it is exhausted after the first pass. Re-call the generator function to create a new one.

    

  

  
Q4. range(5) vs list(range(5)) — memory?
    
Show answer
      
range(5) is a lazy object (O(1) memory). list(range(5)) allocates all 5 ints in memory.

    

  

  
Q5. yield from iterable does what?
    
Show answer
      
Yields each item from iterable one at a time, forwarding send()/throw() transparently.

    

  

  
Q6. next(gen) on exhausted generator raises?
    
Show answer
      
StopIteration — or returns the default if supplied: next(gen, 'done').

    

  

  
Q7. What is a generator expression?
    
Show answer
      
(expr for x in iterable) — lazy generator using comprehension syntax without square brackets.

    

  




Interview — questions & answers
Q: Generator vs list?
A: A list stores all values at once. A generator produces one value at a time — lower memory, lazy evaluation (Real Python).
Q: When does a file reader MemoryError?
A: When you load the whole file into a list (read().split()). Fix: for line in f: yield line so only one line is in memory.
Q: What does yield do?
A: Pauses the function, returns a value to the caller, and saves state. Next next() or loop iteration resumes after the yield. Using return instead ends after one value.
Q: What is a generator expression?
A: Like a list comprehension but with parentheses: (x*x for x in range(10**6)) — lazy, does not build the full list.
Q: What is StopIteration?
A: Raised when a generator is exhausted. for loops catch it automatically to end iteration.

Definition
A decorator wraps a function or class to add behavior without changing its source.
  • Syntax: @timer above def work() means work = timer(work).
  • How: nested function + closure · use functools.wraps to keep __name__ / __doc__.
  • Real use: FastAPI routes @app.get('/') · logging · timing · auth checks.

Key terms explained

Real-life example: Cross-cutting concerns: Decorators wrap once — retry, auth, timing — each layer with input → output.
1) timer decorator — measure runtime
Wraps any function: record start, call original, print elapsed seconds.
# INPUT
import time
from functools import wraps

def timer(fn):
    @wraps(fn)
    def wrapper(*args, **kwargs):
        start = time.time()
        result = fn(*args, **kwargs)
        print(f"{fn.__name__} took {time.time() - start:.2f}s")
        return result
    return wrapper
# OUTPUT (same line as each print)








(wrapper ready — can decorate any function)


2) Apply @timer to run_query
Same function body; decorator adds timing without changing business logic.
# INPUT
@timer
def run_query():
    time.sleep(0.1)
    return "ok"

result = run_query()
# OUTPUT (same line as each print)





run_query took 0.10s
result → 'ok'
Step-by-step (beginner friendly)
  • Step 1 — Function decorators
    A decorator wraps a function to add behavior without changing its source. @decorator is syntactic sugar for func = decorator(func).
    import time

def timer(func):
    def wrapper(*args, **kwargs):
        start = time.time()
        result = func(*args, **kwargs)
        print(f"took {time.time()-start:.2f}s")
        return result
    return wrapper

@timer
def work():
    time.sleep(0.1)
  • Step 2 — Class decorators
    A decorator can wrap a class — modify or register it before use.
    def add_repr(cls):
    def __repr__(self):
        return f"{cls.__name__}()"
    cls.__repr__ = __repr__
    return cls

@add_repr
class User:
    pass

User()   # repr: User()
  • Step 3 — functools.wraps
    Without @wraps, the wrapper hides the original function's name and docstring.
    from functools import wraps

def my_decorator(func):
    @wraps(func)
    def wrapper(*args, **kwargs):
        return func(*args, **kwargs)
    return wrapper

@my_decorator
def greet():
    """Say hello"""
    pass

greet.__name__   # greet (not wrapper)
greet.__doc__    # Say hello


Python keywords — deeper look


@decorator = syntactic sugar: @dec above def f means f = dec(f).
Use when: add logging, timing, auth, route registration without changing f's body.


@wraps(func) = keep original function __name__ and __doc__ on the wrapper.
Always use with custom decorators.


      

When to use which — scenarios




ScenarioUseWhy


Add logging/timing without changing function bodydecoratorCross-cutting concern — wrap any function


Register HTTP route (FastAPI/Flask)@app.get()Framework uses decorators for routing


Enforce auth before handler runs@login_requiredDecorator checks then calls original


Cache expensive function results@lru_cacheBuilt-in functools decorator


Stack multiple behaviorsnested decorators@a @b def f — order matters


Decorator needs configurationdecorator factory@repeat(3) — extra wrapper level





@wraps(fn) preserves the original function name and docstring — always use it in decorators.




Common mistakes


❌ Mistake 1 — not using @wraps(func)Without @wraps, the wrapped function loses its original __name__, __doc__, and other metadata.
❌ Bug
import functools

def my_dec(func):
    def wrapper(*args, **kwargs):
        print("before")
        return func(*args, **kwargs)
    return wrapper  # wrapper.__name__ == "wrapper"

@my_dec
def greet(): pass
print(greet.__name__)  # "wrapper" ← wrong
✔ Fix
import functools

def my_dec(func):
    @functools.wraps(func)  # preserves metadata
    def wrapper(*args, **kwargs):
        print("before")
        return func(*args, **kwargs)
    return wrapper

@my_dec
def greet(): pass
print(greet.__name__)  # "greet" ← correct
💡 Always add @functools.wraps(func) to the inner wrapper. It also ensures help(), inspect, and FastAPI route introspection work correctly.


❌ Mistake 2 — decorator stacking order confusionDecorators apply bottom-up: the decorator closest to the function is applied first.
❌ Bug
@timer
@logger
def process(): ...

# Applied order:
# process = logger(process)  ← first
# process = timer(process)   ← second (outer)
# Confuse this and your timing/logging wraps incorrectly
✔ Fix
# Remember: bottom-up execution
@outer_dec    # applied second — wraps the result of inner_dec
@inner_dec    # applied first — wraps the raw function
def my_func(): ...
# Equivalent to: my_func = outer_dec(inner_dec(my_func))
💡 Read stacked decorators from bottom to top to understand application order. The bottom-most decorator is closest to the function.


❌ Mistake 3 — forgetting () on a decorator factoryA decorator factory is a function that returns a decorator. You must call it with () even if there are no arguments.
❌ Bug
@retry
def call_api(): ...

# If retry is a decorator FACTORY:
def retry(max=3):
    def decorator(func):
        ...
    return decorator

# @retry without () passes the function to retry()
# and retry() returns a decorator, not a function!
✔ Fix
# Decorator factory — must use ():
@retry(max=3)
def call_api(): ...

# @retry() ← always needed for factories
# even @retry() with no args if retry is a factory
💡 If a decorator accepts configuration arguments, it must be called with (). If not called, the function is passed as the first argument to the factory.


Before → After (Pythonic)



  
❌ Copy-paste boilerplate
def create_user(data):
    try:
        return db.insert(data)
    except DBError as e:
        logger.error(e); raise

def update_user(id, data):
    try:                         # same boilerplate!
        return db.update(id, data)
    except DBError as e:
        logger.error(e); raise

  
→

  
✔ Decorator
import functools

def db_errors(func):
    @functools.wraps(func)
    def wrapper(*args, **kwargs):
        try:
            return func(*args, **kwargs)
        except DBError as e:
            logger.error(e); raise
    return wrapper

@db_errors
def create_user(data): return db.insert(data)

@db_errors
def update_user(id, data): return db.update(id, data)




Self-check quiz



  
Q1. @decorator is syntactic sugar for?
    
Show answer
      
func = decorator(func) — the decorator is called with the function and the result replaces the function name.

    

  

  
Q2. Why use @functools.wraps(func)?
    
Show answer
      
Preserves the wrapped function's __name__, __doc__, and other attributes on the wrapper.

    

  

  
Q3. @dec1 @dec2 def f(): — which decorator is applied first?
    
Show answer
      
dec2 (bottom-up). Equivalent to f = dec1(dec2(f)).

    

  

  
Q4. A decorator factory is?
    
Show answer
      
A function that returns a decorator, e.g. @retry(max=3) — retry is the factory, retry(max=3) returns the actual decorator.

    

  

  
Q5. What does functools.partial do?
    
Show answer
      
Creates a new function with some arguments pre-filled: add5 = partial(add, 5).

    

  

  
Q6. @property is itself what kind of object?
    
Show answer
      
A built-in descriptor that turns a method into a computed attribute.

    

  

  
Q7. Can a decorator be applied to a class (not just a function)?
    
Show answer
      
Yes — @dataclass is a class decorator that modifies the class in place.

    

  




Interview — questions & answers
Q: Explain decorators in simple terms.
A: A decorator is a function that takes a function and returns a new function with extra behavior. FastAPI uses @app.get('/') to register routes.
Q: Why use functools.wraps?
A: Without it, the wrapped function loses its original __name__ and __doc__ — bad for debugging, introspection, and docs.
Q: Can a decorator accept arguments?
A: Yes — use a factory: def repeat(n): def decorator(func): ... return decorator. Then @repeat(3).
Q: Decorator vs inheritance for extending behavior?
A: Decorators compose behavior around a single function at runtime. Inheritance models is-a relationships between types.

Step-by-step (beginner friendly)
  • Step 1 — try, except, else & finally
    Handle errors gracefully. else runs if no exception. finally always runs.

Python keywords — deeper look


try / except / else / finally
except: handle error.
else: runs if no exception in try (not the same as loop else!).
finally: always runs — cleanup.


raise = throw an exception. raise ... from ... = chain cause for debugging.
Custom Exception = class AppError(Exception): pass

ScenarioUseWhy


Expected failure (bad user input)try/except ValueErrorCatch specific type — not bare except:


Cleanup must run (close file, release lock)finally or withRuns even if exception raised

Common mistakes


❌ Mistake 1 — bare except: catches everythingBare except: catches BaseException including SystemExit and KeyboardInterrupt, preventing clean program shutdown.
❌ Bug
try:
    result = risky()
except:      # catches SystemExit, KeyboardInterrupt!
    pass       # silently swallows ALL exceptions
✔ Fix
try:
    result = risky()
except ValueError as e:
    logger.warning("Invalid value: %s", e)
except Exception as e:     # catchall for non-system
    logger.error("Unexpected: %s", e)
    raise
💡 Use the most specific exception type first. A bare except should only appear in top-level error boundaries (CLI entry points) and always re-raises or logs.


❌ Mistake 2 — raise e vs raise (traceback loss)raise e in an except block resets the traceback to the current line. raise alone preserves the original location.
❌ Bug
try:
    risky()
except Exception as e:
    raise e   # traceback starts HERE — original lost!
✔ Fix
try:
    risky()
except Exception as e:
    logger.error(e)
    raise     # re-raises with ORIGINAL traceback preserved
💡 Use bare raise to re-raise. If you need to raise a different exception, use raise NewError(...) from e to chain them.


❌ Mistake 3 — catching too broadly and swallowing errorsexcept Exception: pass silently discards errors, making debugging nearly impossible.
❌ Bug
def load_config(path):
    try:
        with open(path) as f:
            return json.load(f)
    except Exception:
        pass   # all errors silently ignored!
✔ Fix
def load_config(path):
    try:
        with open(path, encoding="utf-8") as f:
            return json.load(f)
    except FileNotFoundError:
        return {}   # expected: file not created yet
    except json.JSONDecodeError as e:
        raise ValueError(f"Bad config: {path}") from e
💡 Only catch exceptions you can handle meaningfully. Let unexpected exceptions propagate so they can be fixed.


Before → After (Pythonic)



  
❌ Swallowing exceptions
def get_user(id):
    try:
        return db.query(id)
    except:
        return None   # was it NotFound? DBDown? TypeError?
                      # impossible to tell!

  
→

  
✔ Precise handling
class NotFoundError(Exception): pass

def get_user(id):
    try:
        return db.query(id)
    except db.NotFound:
        raise NotFoundError(f"User {id} not found")
    except db.ConnectionError:
        raise  # re-raise — caller handles infra errors




Self-check quiz



  
Q1. except Exception vs bare except: — what extra does bare catch?
    
Show answer
      
Bare except: also catches SystemExit, KeyboardInterrupt, and GeneratorExit (all BaseException subclasses).

    

  

  
Q2. raise vs raise e in an except block?
    
Show answer
      
raise preserves the original traceback. raise e resets the traceback origin to the current line.

    

  

  
Q3. finally block runs when?
    
Show answer
      
Always — whether an exception was raised, caught, or not. Even after a return in the try block.

    

  

  
Q4. except (TypeError, ValueError): catches?
    
Show answer
      
Either TypeError or ValueError — any of the listed exception types.

    

  

  
Q5. Custom exception should inherit from?
    
Show answer
      
Exception (not BaseException), so it's caught by except Exception: but not by bare except:.

    

  

  
Q6. raise NewError('msg') from original_err does what?
    
Show answer
      
Raises NewError while chaining the original exception, preserving both tracebacks in the output.

    

  

  
Q7. What is exception chaining? How to suppress it?
    
Show answer
      
Automatic when an exception is raised inside an except block. Suppress with raise NewError() from None.

    

  




Interview — questions & answers
Q: Why not use bare except?
A: It catches everything including KeyboardInterrupt and hides the real bug. Catch specific exceptions you can handle.
Q: What does raise from do?
A: Chains exceptions — the new error keeps a link to the original cause in the traceback (__cause__).
Q: When does else run in try/except?
A: Only when the try block completes without raising any exception.
Q: finally vs else?
A: else runs on success only. finally runs always — use for cleanup like closing connections.

Threading & GIL

  
Concurrency runs overlapping work — threads share one process; processes get separate memory. thread…

Definition
Concurrency runs overlapping work — threads share one process; processes get separate memory.
  • threading: good for I/O · limited by the GIL for CPU-bound work · use Lock against races.
  • multiprocessing / futures: ProcessPoolExecutor for CPU · ThreadPoolExecutor for I/O.
  • Pick: I/O wait → threads · heavy CPU math → processes.


Decision flowchart


Read from the top. If the answer is YES, stop at that box. If NO, go down.



  

    
I want work to happen “at the same time”Threads vs processes — and the GIL gate

    

    
      

        
Is the program mostly waiting (network, disk)?

        

          

          
NO

          

            YES
            

            

              Use threading
              While one waits, another can run. Good for I/O.
              threading.Thread
            

          

        

      

      

        
Is the program crunching heavy CPU math?

        

          

          
NO

          

            YES
            

            

              Use multiprocessing
              Separate processes — better for pure CPU work.
              ProcessPool
            

          

        

      

      

        
Wonder why two threads don’t both burn CPU hard?

        

          

          
NO

          

            YES
            

            

              Remember the GIL
              CPython mostly runs one bytecode thread at a time.
              GIL · one at a time
            

          

        

      

    

    

      Simple rule
      Waiting a lot → threads. Heavy math → processes.
      I/O → threads · CPU → processes
    

  





Concurrency — pick the tool



  
What is the work waiting on?

  

  
I/O waitthreading · ThreadPoolExecutor (GIL OK)
CPU heavymultiprocessing · ProcessPoolExecutor
Many socketsasyncio (see next slide)

  
GIL = one Python bytecode thread at a time.





GIL impact



  

    
I/O-bound (OK)

    
  • Download / wait DB
  • threading fine
  • Threads release GIL while waiting

  

  
vs

  

    
CPU-bound (not OK)

    
  • Heavy math
  • Use processes
  • Bypass GIL

  

  




Key terms explained




TermMeaningQuick example


ThreadLightweight concurrent execution within one process.threading.Thread


GILGlobal Interpreter Lock — one thread runs Python bytecode at a time.CPython limitation


LockMutex preventing two threads mutating shared data simultaneously.with lock:


I/O-boundWaiting on network/disk — threads help despite GIL.HTTP requests


CPU-boundHeavy computation — use multiprocessing not threads.image processing


ThreadPoolExecutorPool of worker threads for parallel I/O tasks.concurrent.futures


Real-life example: Image resize service: Threads for download (I/O); processes for CPU work — each pool with input → output.
1) ThreadPoolExecutor — parallel downloads
Network waits release the GIL — threads are fine for I/O-bound fetch.
# INPUT
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor

urls = ["http://a/img1.jpg", "http://b/img2.jpg"]

with ThreadPoolExecutor() as pool:
    images = list(pool.map(download, urls))
# OUTPUT (same line as each print)





images → [bytes1, bytes2]  (downloaded concurrently)
2) ProcessPoolExecutor — CPU resize
Pixel crunching needs real parallel cores — separate processes bypass the GIL.
# INPUT
from concurrent.futures import ProcessPoolExecutor

with ProcessPoolExecutor() as pool:
    out = list(pool.map(heavy_resize, images))
# OUTPUT (same line as each print)



out → [resized1, resized2]  (CPU work on multiple cores)
Step-by-step (beginner friendly)
  • Step 1 — threading.Thread & Lock
    Threads share memory within one process. Use Lock to prevent race conditions.
    import threading

counter = 0
lock = threading.Lock()

def increment():
    global counter
    with lock:
        counter += 1

t = threading.Thread(target=increment)
t.start()
t.join()
  • Step 2 — GIL
    Global Interpreter Lock — only one thread executes Python bytecode at a time in CPython.
    Task typeThreads help?
    I/O-bound (network, disk)Yes
    CPU-bound (math, parsing)No — use multiprocessing
    Why I/O works: threads release the GIL while waiting on I/O.
  • Step 3 — multiprocessing workaround
    Separate processes bypass the GIL — each has its own Python interpreter and memory.
    from multiprocessing import Process

def heavy(n):
    print(sum(i*i for i in range(n)))

if __name__ == "__main__":
    p = Process(target=heavy, args=(1_000_000,))
    p.start()
    p.join()
  • Step 4 — concurrent.futures
    High-level API for thread and process pools.
    from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor, ProcessPoolExecutor

with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=4) as pool:
    results = list(pool.map(fetch_url, urls))

with ProcessPoolExecutor() as pool:
    results = list(pool.map(compute, big_jobs))


Python keywords — deeper look


GIL (Global Interpreter Lock) = only one thread runs Python bytecode at a time in CPython.
Good for: I/O (network, disk).
Bad for: CPU-heavy math in threads — use multiprocessing.


Lock = mutex — only one thread enters critical section at a time.
with lock:
    shared_counter += 1


      

When to use which — scenarios




ScenarioUseWhy


Many HTTP requests, file downloadsthreading / ThreadPoolI/O-bound — GIL released during wait


Heavy math, image processing, ML trainingmultiprocessingCPU-bound — bypass GIL with separate processes


Shared counter without race conditionthreading.LockMutex around critical section


Simple parallel I/O tasksThreadPoolExecutorPool manages thread lifecycle


Parallel CPU on all coresProcessPoolExecutorTrue parallelism — separate memory


Async HTTP (thousands of connections)asyncioEven better than threads for I/O scale




GIL: Global Interpreter Lock — only one thread runs Python bytecode at a time. Good for I/O-bound tasks; use multiprocessing for CPU-bound work.





Common mistakes


❌ Mistake 1 — using threads for CPU-bound tasks (GIL blocks parallelism)The GIL allows only one thread to execute Python bytecode at a time. Threads do not speed up CPU-bound work.
❌ Bug
from threading import Thread

def crunch(n):
    return sum(i**2 for i in range(n))

t1 = Thread(target=crunch, args=(10**7,))
t2 = Thread(target=crunch, args=(10**7,))
t1.start(); t2.start()
t1.join(); t2.join()
# NOT faster than sequential due to GIL
✔ Fix
from multiprocessing import Pool

def crunch(n):
    return sum(i**2 for i in range(n))

with Pool(2) as p:
    results = p.map(crunch, [10**7, 10**7])
# Truly parallel — each process has its own GIL
💡 Use threading for I/O-bound tasks (network, file, DB). Use multiprocessing or concurrent.futures.ProcessPoolExecutor for CPU-bound work.


❌ Mistake 2 — shared mutable state without a LockTwo threads incrementing a shared counter without a lock produce a race condition — the result is non-deterministic.
❌ Bug
import threading
counter = 0

def increment():
    global counter
    for _ in range(100000):
        counter += 1  # read-modify-write is not atomic!

t1 = threading.Thread(target=increment)
t2 = threading.Thread(target=increment)
t1.start(); t2.start()
t1.join(); t2.join()
print(counter)  # not always 200000!
✔ Fix
import threading
counter = 0
lock = threading.Lock()

def increment():
    global counter
    for _ in range(100000):
        with lock:
            counter += 1  # protected

# Now counter == 200000 always
💡 Any shared mutable state accessed by multiple threads requires a Lock. Prefer threading.local() or queue.Queue to avoid shared state entirely.


❌ Mistake 3 — not joining threads before using their resultsIf the main thread proceeds before worker threads finish, results may be incomplete or incorrect.
❌ Bug
results = []
t = threading.Thread(target=lambda: results.append(compute()))
t.start()
print(results)  # [] — thread hasn't finished yet!
✔ Fix
results = []
t = threading.Thread(target=lambda: results.append(compute()))
t.start()
t.join()         # wait for thread to finish
print(results)  # [computed_value]
💡 Always .join() threads before using their results. Use concurrent.futures.ThreadPoolExecutor for cleaner result collection.


Before → After (Pythonic)



  
❌ No lock (race condition)
balance = 1000

def withdraw(amount):
    global balance
    if balance >= amount:
        # gap here — another thread can run!
        balance -= amount

# Two threads withdrawing simultaneously
# can overdraft the account!

  
→

  
✔ With Lock (thread-safe)
import threading
balance = 1000
lock = threading.Lock()

def withdraw(amount):
    global balance
    with lock:          # atomic section
        if balance >= amount:
            balance -= amount
            return True
    return False




Self-check quiz



  
Q1. What is the GIL?
    
Show answer
      
The Global Interpreter Lock — a mutex that allows only one thread to execute Python bytecode at a time.

    

  

  
Q2. Threads are best for?
    
Show answer
      
I/O-bound tasks (network requests, file reads) where threads wait rather than compute.

    

  

  
Q3. multiprocessing is better for?
    
Show answer
      
CPU-bound tasks — each process gets its own GIL and can run in true parallel.

    

  

  
Q4. What is a race condition?
    
Show answer
      
Two threads read and modify shared data simultaneously, producing non-deterministic results.

    

  

  
Q5. thread.join() does what?
    
Show answer
      
Blocks the calling thread until the target thread finishes.

    

  

  
Q6. threading.Lock() purpose?
    
Show answer
      
Ensures only one thread at a time can execute the protected code block.

    

  

  
Q7. queue.Queue is thread-safe — why prefer it over a list?
    
Show answer
      
Queue has internal locking; a plain list does not. .put()/.get() are atomic.

    

  




Interview — questions & answers
Q: What is the GIL?
A: A lock in CPython so only one thread executes Python bytecode at a time. I/O-bound tasks still benefit from threads; CPU-bound tasks need multiprocessing.
Q: Thread vs process?
A: Thread: shared memory, lightweight, GIL-limited for CPU. Process: separate memory, heavier, true parallelism for CPU work.
Q: Why if __name__ == "__main__" for multiprocessing?
A: On Windows, child processes re-import the module. Without the guard, code at module level runs again in each child — causing infinite spawn loops.
Q: ThreadPoolExecutor vs manual threads?
A: Executor manages a pool, queues work, and returns futures. Cleaner than manually creating and joining many threads.

Async / Await

  
asyncio runs many I/O-bound tasks on one thread using an event loop — concurrency, not CPU paralleli…

Definition
asyncio runs many I/O-bound tasks on one thread using an event loop — concurrency, not CPU parallelism.
  • Keywords: async def (coroutine) · await (pause until ready) · asyncio.gather (run many together).
  • Start: asyncio.run(main()) · also async with / async for.
  • Trap: don’t call blocking I/O inside async code — FastAPI can use async def endpoints for non-blocking DB/HTTP.


Decision flowchart


Read from the top. If the answer is YES, stop at that box. If NO, go down.



  

    
Many waits, one friendly styleasync/await — take turns while waiting

    

    
      

        
Lots of network waits in one program?

        

          

          
NO

          

            YES
            

            

              Write async def + await
              Pause this task while waiting; let others run.
              async def fetch():    await ...
            

          

        

      

      

        
Run many async jobs together?

        

          

          
NO

          

            YES
            

            

              asyncio.gather
              Start a group of tasks and wait for all.
              await gather(t1, t2)
            

          

        

      

      

        
Who decides whose turn it is?

        

          

          
NO

          

            YES
            

            

              The event loop
              A traffic officer for async tasks.
              asyncio.run(main())
            

          

        

      

    

    

      Rule
      You can only await inside an async function.
      await only in async def

↺

  
Do not call blocking I/O inside async code.





Sync vs async



  

    
Sync def

    
  • One call waits
  • Simple
  • Blocks the thread

  

  
vs

  • Many tasks
  • One event loop

  

  




Key terms explained




TermMeaningQuick example


async defDefines a coroutine function — not run until awaited. async def fetch():


awaitPause coroutine until async operation completes. await asyncio.sleep(1)


CoroutineCooperative task managed by event loop.async function


Event loopSchedules and runs coroutines — asyncio.run() starts it.asyncio.run(main())


asyncio.gatherRun multiple coroutines concurrently, wait for all.await gather(a(), b())


ConcurrencyMultiple tasks making progress — not same as parallel CPU.async HTTP calls


Real-life example: Notification fan-out: Three network calls concurrently with gather — each async step with input → output.
1) Individual async senders
Each channel awaits a short sleep (stand-in for a real HTTP call).
# INPUT
import asyncio

async def send_email():
    await asyncio.sleep(0.2)
    return "email ok"

async def send_sms():
    await asyncio.sleep(0.2)
    return "sms ok"
# OUTPUT (same line as each print)








(coroutines defined — not run until awaited)
2) asyncio.gather — run all three together
Total wait ≈ 0.2s (longest task), not 0.6s sequential.
# INPUT
async def notify():
    results = await asyncio.gather(
        send_email(),
        send_sms(),
        push(),
    )
    return results

asyncio.run(notify())
# OUTPUT (same line as each print)








results → ['email ok', 'sms ok', 'push ok']
Step-by-step (beginner friendly)
  • Step 1 — asyncio event loop
    The loop schedules and runs coroutines cooperatively on one thread — ideal for many concurrent I/O waits.
    import asyncio

async def main():
    print("start")
    await asyncio.sleep(1)
    print("done")

asyncio.run(main())   # creates and runs the loop
  • Step 2 — async def, await & coroutines
    async def defines a coroutine. await pauses until that operation completes — only inside async def.
    async def fetch(url):
    await asyncio.sleep(0.5)   # simulate I/O
    return f"data from {url}"

async def main():
    result = await fetch("api/users")
    print(result)
  • Step 3 — asyncio.gather & asyncio.run
    gather runs multiple coroutines concurrently. run is the entry point.
    async def main():
    results = await asyncio.gather(
        fetch("/a"),
        fetch("/b"),
        fetch("/c"),
    )
    print(results)

asyncio.run(main())
  • Step 4 — Async context managers & iterators
    Async versions of with and for for non-blocking I/O resources.
    class AsyncResource:
    async def __aenter__(self):
        await connect()
        return self
    async def __aexit__(self, *args):
        await disconnect()

async def main():
    async with AsyncResource() as r:
        async for item in r.stream():
            process(item)


Python keywords — deeper look


async def = defines a coroutine — does not run until awaited.
await = pause until I/O completes — only valid inside async def.


asyncio.run(main()) = start the event loop once from synchronous code.
Trap: never use time.sleep in async code — use await asyncio.sleep.


      

When to use which — scenarios




ScenarioUseWhy


Thousands of concurrent HTTP/API callsasyncioSingle thread, non-blocking I/O


Sequential awaits (each depends on prior)await one by oneWhen step 2 needs result of step 1


Independent I/O tasks in parallelasyncio.gatherAll run concurrently — ~1x slowest


CPU-heavy image resize loopmultiprocessingasync does NOT help CPU-bound work


FastAPI endpoint calling DB + HTTPasync def routeNon-blocking while waiting


Simple script with one requestsync requestsasync overhead not worth it





Use async for I/O-bound concurrency (HTTP, DB, files). Do not use for CPU-heavy work — use multiprocessing instead.




Common mistakes


❌ Mistake 1 — calling a coroutine without awaitCalling an async def function without await returns a coroutine object — the function body does not run.
❌ Bug
import asyncio

async def fetch():
    return "data"

result = fetch()   # coroutine object — not executed!
print(result)      # <coroutine object fetch at 0x...>
✔ Fix
import asyncio

async def fetch():
    return "data"

async def main():
    result = await fetch()  # now it runs
    print(result)           # "data"

asyncio.run(main())
💡 If you forget await, Python will typically warn: RuntimeWarning: coroutine ‘fetch’ was never awaited.


❌ Mistake 2 — using blocking calls inside async defBlocking operations (like time.sleep() or requests.get()) freeze the entire event loop, preventing all other coroutines from running.
❌ Bug
import asyncio, time

async def slow_fetch():
    time.sleep(2)    # BLOCKS the event loop!
    return "data"
✔ Fix
import asyncio, httpx

async def slow_fetch():
    await asyncio.sleep(2)   # yields control
    async with httpx.AsyncClient() as client:
        resp = await client.get("https://api.example.com")
    return resp.json()
💡 Use async-native libraries: httpx or aiohttp (not requests), asyncio.sleep() (not time.sleep()), async DB drivers.


❌ Mistake 3 — asyncio.run() inside an already running event loopIn Jupyter notebooks and some frameworks, an event loop is already running. Calling asyncio.run() raises RuntimeError.
❌ Bug
# In Jupyter notebook:
async def main(): return "done"
asyncio.run(main())
# RuntimeError: This event loop is already running
✔ Fix
# In Jupyter — use await directly:
result = await main()   # no asyncio.run() needed

# In scripts:
asyncio.run(main())     # correct for script entry point
💡 In Jupyter, use await directly in cells. In FastAPI, define route handlers as async def and the framework manages the loop.


Before → After (Pythonic)



  
❌ Blocking in async context
import time
import asyncio

async def process_items(items):
    results = []
    for item in items:
        time.sleep(0.1)        # blocks loop!
        results.append(item * 2)
    return results

  
→

  
✔ Non-blocking with gather
import asyncio

async def process_item(item):
    await asyncio.sleep(0.1)   # yields
    return item * 2

async def process_items(items):
    tasks = [process_item(x) for x in items]
    return await asyncio.gather(*tasks)  # concurrent




Self-check quiz



  
Q1. Calling async def f(): without await returns?
    
Show answer
      
A coroutine object — the function body does not run. Python warns: coroutine was never awaited.

    

  

  
Q2. await f() — what does await do?
    
Show answer
      
Suspends the current coroutine, yields control to the event loop, and resumes when f() completes.

    

  

  
Q3. How to run a coroutine from synchronous code?
    
Show answer
      
asyncio.run(coroutine()) — creates an event loop, runs the coroutine, and closes the loop.

    

  

  
Q4. time.sleep() vs asyncio.sleep() in async code?
    
Show answer
      
asyncio.sleep() yields to the event loop (non-blocking). time.sleep() blocks the entire loop.

    

  

  
Q5. asyncio.gather(*tasks) does what?
    
Show answer
      
Runs multiple coroutines concurrently and returns all results when all finish.

    

  

  
Q6. What is the event loop?
    
Show answer
      
A scheduler that manages and runs async tasks — one coroutine runs at a time but others are resumed when awaited operations complete.

    

  

  
Q7. async for is used with?
    
Show answer
      
Async iterables — objects implementing __aiter__ and __anext__, e.g. async DB cursors, SSE streams.

    

  




Interview — questions & answers
Q: async vs threading?
A: Threading uses OS threads and the GIL. Async uses one thread and cooperatively switches during awaits — great for many concurrent I/O connections.
Q: Can you use time.sleep in async code?
A: No — it blocks the whole event loop. Use await asyncio.sleep() instead.
Q: When NOT to use async?
A: CPU-heavy work blocks the loop. Use threads, multiprocessing, or run CPU work in asyncio.to_thread().
Q: What does asyncio.gather do?
A: Runs multiple coroutines concurrently and returns results in order. If one fails, others may still complete depending on options.

Definition
The logging module is production output — levels, timestamps, and routing to files/agents (not print).
  • Levels: DEBUG → INFO → WARNING → ERROR → CRITICAL.
  • Pattern: logging.getLogger(__name__) · INFO in prod · logger.exception inside except.
  • Handlers: console · RotatingFileHandler · lazy % formatting.


Decision flowchart


Read from the top. If the answer is YES, stop at that box. If NO, go down.

NO

          

            YES
            

            

              Pick a level
              DEBUG (chatty) up to CRITICAL (fire alarm).
              DEBUG → INFO → WARNING → ERROR → CRITICAL
            

          

        

      

      

        
Where should messages go?

        

          

          
NO

          

            YES
            

            

              Add handlers
              Screen, file, or rotating files that don’t grow forever.
              StreamHandlerRotatingFileHandler
            

          

        

      

      

        
Do you want a clear message format?

        

          

          
NO

          

            YES
            

            

              Use a formatter
              Show time, level, and text the same way every time.
              %(levelname)s %(message)s
            

          

        

      

    

    

      Prefer logging
      In real apps, logging beats print — you can filter and save it.
      logging > print

Prefer logger.info("x=%s", x) over f-strings when filtered.



print vs logging

Key terms explained
