C# Comparison — Memory: refcount, GC, weakref, del



  Why does Python talk about so many memory words?
  CPython uses more than one cleanup plan at once.
  C# mostly uses one big garbage collector, plus a few helpers.





TermPython (CPython)C# (.NET)



  Reference counting
  Each object keeps a count of how many names/boxes point to it.
  When the count hits 0, it is freed right away.
  Check with sys.getrefcount(x) (count looks a bit high because of the call itself).
  Not the main plan. .NET does not free objects by a visible per-object refcount
  in everyday code. The CLR GC finds unused objects later.




  Garbage collector
  Extra cleaner for circles (A→B→A) that refcount alone cannot free.
  Call gc.collect() (usually automatic).
  This is the main cleanup. Mark / sweep style GC runs in generations.
  You rarely call GC.Collect() yourself.




  Generation (GC)
  Buckets for young vs older objects: gen 0, 1, 2.
  Young objects are checked more often.
  Same idea: Gen 0, 1, 2. Short-lived objects die in Gen 0 most of the time.




  weakref
  A soft pointer: you can look at the object, but you do not keep it alive.
  Good for caches. weakref.ref(obj)
  WeakReference / WeakReference<T> — same idea for caches
  without pinning memory forever.




  del
  Removes a name from the namespace (del x).
  If that was the last strong reference, refcount can free the object soon.
  No everyday del for locals.
  Use scope end, using / IDisposable for files/handles,
  and let the GC reclaim managed memory.





Why Python lists more tools
Python
refcount (fast) + cyclic GC (for circles) + weakref + del
vs
C#
mainly CLR GC + WeakReference + IDisposable / using


Picture


    
  
  • Python: sticky-note counter on each toy (refcount). When nobody holds it, throw it away now.
  If two toys hold each other in a loop, a special cleaner (GC) comes later.
    • 
  
  • C#: a janitor (GC) walks the room later and throws away toys nobody can reach.
  You still close files yourself with using.
    • 




What does each line do? (full detail)




  1) weakref.ref(a) — soft look
  

    Creates a weak reference to object a and stores that soft pointer in soft_ref.
  

  
    
    
  • Does NOT add +1 to the object’s strong refcount (unlike a normal name).
    • 
    
  • So by itself, it does not keep the object alive.
    • 
    
  • Later you can ask: obj = soft_ref()
      — if the object still exists → you get it;
      if it was already freed → you get None.
    • 
    
  • Why use it? Caches / maps that should remember something only while someone else still needs it.
    • 
    
  • C# twin: WeakReference<T> / WeakReference.
    • 
  






  2) del a, b — drop the names
  

    del removes the names a and b from this scope.
    It does not mean “erase the object’s memory this second” by itself.
  

  
    
    
  • Each del drops one strong reference (refcount −1 for that binding).
    • 
    
  • If refcount hits 0 → CPython frees the object immediately.
    • 
    
  • In the sample, a and b still point to each other (a.other = b, b.other = a),
      so after del a, b the objects may still have refcount ≥ 1 from the circle.
      Refcount alone cannot free them.
    • 
    
  • Also: del works on names, list slots, dict keys (del d["k"]), attributes, etc.
    • 
    
  • C# twin: no everyday del for locals — leave scope, or using for resources.
    • 
  






  3) gc.collect() — run the circle cleaner now
  

    Asks Python’s cyclic garbage collector to run right now
    (normally it runs automatically in the background).
  

  
    
    
  • Finds groups of objects that only point to each other and are not reachable from your program.
    • 
    
  • Those circles are freed even though each object’s refcount was never 0.
    • 
    
  • Returns how many objects it collected (an int).
    • 
    
  • You usually do not need to call it in app code — useful for demos, tests, or hunting leaks.
    • 
    
  • C# twin: GC.Collect() — also rare in production; prefer letting the runtime decide.
    • 
  





Python — walk the three steps in order:


1import gc, weakref


2 


3class Node:


4    def __init__(self, name):


5        self.name = name


6        self.other = None


7 


8a = Node("A")


9b = Node("B")


10a.other = b


11b.other = a              # circle A ↔ B


12 


13soft_ref = weakref.ref(a)   # 1) soft look — no strong keep-alive by itself


14print(soft_ref())           # still alive → Node A (names a/b exist)


15 


16del a, b                 # 2) drop strong names; circle may remain


17print(soft_ref())           # may still be Node, or None after GC


18 


19n = gc.collect()         # 3) force cyclic GC now


20print(n, soft_ref())        # collected count; soft_ref() often None now


C# — WeakReference + using (no del / rare GC.Collect):


1using System;


2using System.IO;


3 


4var softRef = new WeakReference<string>("hello");


5if (softRef.TryGetTarget(out var text))


6    Console.WriteLine(text);  // soft look


7 


8using (var reader = File.OpenText("data.txt"))


9{


10    Console.WriteLine(reader.ReadLine());


11}  // Dispose closes the file — do not rely on GC for handles


12 


13// GC.Collect();  // possible, but avoid in normal apps




Bottom line: weakref.ref = soft peek (no keep-alive). del = drop a strong name (may free if refcount hits 0). gc.collect() = run cyclic GC now (for unreachable circles). Python lists many tools because it mixes refcount + cyclic GC; C# mostly uses one GC + WeakReference + using.

C# Comparison — Pydantic vs DataAnnotations / FluentValidation


API validation
Python
Pydantic BaseModel + Field + field_validator → ValidationError → FastAPI HTTP 422
vs
C#
C# record / DTO + DataAnnotations (or FluentValidation) → ModelState → often HTTP 400




Python (Pydantic)C# twin



  BaseModel — typed schema; validates on build
  record / DTO class + model binding




  Field(ge=18) — built-in constraint
  [Range(18, 120)] or FluentValidation GreaterThanOrEqualTo(18)




  @field_validator("email") — custom rule (runs automatically)
  Custom ValidationAttribute, or FluentValidation RuleFor(x => x.Email)




  model_validate(dict)
  ASP.NET model binding from JSON body




  ValidationError → FastAPI HTTP 422
  Invalid ModelState → often HTTP 400 (or ProblemDetails)




  model_dump()
  Serialize DTO / JsonSerializer.Serialize





Python — Pydantic model + auto validators:


1from pydantic import BaseModel, Field, field_validator, ValidationError


2 


3class UserCreate(BaseModel):


4    email: str


5    age: int = Field(ge=18)


6 


7    @field_validator("email")


8    @classmethod


9    def lower_email(cls, v):


10        return v.lower()   # runs automatically on validate


11 


12body = {"email": "Anu@Co.COM", "age": "25"}


13user = UserCreate.model_validate(body)


14print(user.email)   # anu@co.com


15 


16try:


17    UserCreate.model_validate({"email": "x@y.com", "age": 15})


18except ValidationError as e:


19    print(e.errors())   # FastAPI → HTTP 422


C# — DataAnnotations (attributes on the DTO):


1using System.ComponentModel.DataAnnotations;


2 


3public record UserCreate(


4    [Required, EmailAddress] string Email,


5    [Range(18, 120)] int Age


6);


7 


8// ASP.NET Core: bind JSON → UserCreate


9// if (!ModelState.IsValid) return BadRequest(ModelState);  // often 400




C# — FluentValidation (closer to @field_validator — rules in a separate class, runs when you validate):




1using FluentValidation;


2 


3public record UserCreate(string Email, int Age);


4 


5public class UserCreateValidator : AbstractValidator<UserCreate>


6{


7    public UserCreateValidator()


8    {


9        RuleFor(x => x.Email)


10            .NotEmpty()


11            .EmailAddress()


12            .Must(e => e.Contains('@'))


13            .WithMessage("email must contain @");


14 


15        RuleFor(x => x.Age)


16            .GreaterThanOrEqualTo(18);   // like Field(ge=18)


17 


18        // Normalize like lower_email — transform before/after rules:


19        RuleFor(x => x.Email)


20            .Transform(e => e.ToLowerInvariant());


21    }


22}


23 


24var user = new UserCreate("Anu@Co.COM", 25);


25var result = new UserCreateValidator().Validate(user);


26if (!result.IsValid)


27    foreach (var err in result.Errors)


28        Console.WriteLine(err.ErrorMessage);


29// In ASP.NET: services.AddValidatorsFromAssembly... + automatic 400




Bottom line: Pydantic = runtime schema + coercion + validators in one place. C# often uses DataAnnotations on the DTO or FluentValidation (separate validator class — most like field_validator). FastAPI → 422; ASP.NET → often 400.

C# Comparison — Dunder methods vs ToString / Equals / Count
Dunder ≈ C# operator / override hooks
Python
__str__ / __repr__ / __eq__ / __len__
vs
C#
ToString() / debug display / Equals / .Count


Dunder = double underscore. Python calls these when you use built-ins
(print, ==, len). C# uses method overrides and properties
instead of magic names.




PythonTriggered byC# twin



  __str__
  print(obj), str(obj), f-strings
  ToString() — friendly display




  __repr__
  repr(obj), debugger, lists
  No exact twin — often richer ToString(),
  [DebuggerDisplay], or a dedicated debug dump




  __eq__
  a == b
  Equals + often operator == /
  IEquatable<T> (and GetHashCode)




  __len__
  len(obj)
  .Count / .Length property
  (no global len())





Python — Order with four dunders:


1class Order:


2    def __init__(self, order_id, customer, items):


3        self.order_id = order_id


4        self.customer = customer


5        self.items = items


6 


7    def __str__(self):


8        return f"Order #{self.order_id} for {self.customer}"


9 


10    def __repr__(self):


11        return f"Order(order_id={self.order_id!r}, ...)"


12 


13    def __eq__(self, other):


14        if not isinstance(other, Order):


15            return NotImplemented


16        return self.order_id == other.order_id


17 


18    def __len__(self):


19        return len(self.items)


20 


21o = Order(42, "Anu", ["pen", "notebook"])


22print(o)          # __str__


23print(o == Order(42, "X", []))  # __eq__


24print(len(o))     # __len__


C# — same ideas with ToString / Equals / Count:


1class Order : IEquatable<Order>


2{


3    public int OrderId { get; }


4    public string Customer { get; }


5    public List<string> Items { get; }


6 


7    public Order(int orderId, string customer, List<string> items)


8    {


9        OrderId = orderId;


10        Customer = customer;


11        Items = items;


12    }


13 


14    // like __str__ (and often also used as debug text)


15    public override string ToString()


16        => $"Order #{OrderId} for {Customer}";


17 


18    // like __eq__


19    public bool Equals(Order? other)


20        => other is not null && OrderId == other.OrderId;


21 


22    public override bool Equals(object? obj)


23        => Equals(obj as Order);


24 


25    public override int GetHashCode() => OrderId.GetHashCode();


26 


27    public static bool operator ==(Order? a, Order? b)


28        => a is null ? b is null : a.Equals(b);


29 


30    public static bool operator !=(Order? a, Order? b) => !(a == b);


31 


32    // like __len__ — property, not len(order)


33    public int Count => Items.Count;


34}


35 


36var o = new Order(42, "Anu", new() { "pen", "notebook" });


37Console.WriteLine(o);                 // ToString


38Console.WriteLine(o == new Order(42, "X", new()));  // Equals


39Console.WriteLine(o.Count);           // Count


Bottom line: __str__ ≈ ToString(). __eq__ ≈ Equals (+ ==). __len__ ≈ .Count. __repr__ has no single C# twin — keep debug detail in ToString or a debugger attribute.

C# Comparison — OOP: class, self, inheritance, MRO


OOP terms at a glance
Python
class / object / __init__ / self / inheritance / polymorphism / encapsulation / MRO
vs
C#
class / instance / constructor / this / : base / override / private+property / single base + interfaces




Python termMeaningC# twin



  Class
  Blueprint — attributes + methods
  class Dog { } (same idea)




  Object
  Instance created at runtime
  new Dog("Rex") — instance of the class




  __init__
  Initializer — sets up the new object
  Constructor — method named like the class




  self
  Current instance — must be first param
  this — implicit inside instance methods




  Inheritance
  class Dog(Animal): — multiple bases OK
  class Dog : Animal — one base class; extra contracts via interface




  Polymorphism
  Same call, different behavior — often duck typing
  virtual / override, or interface methods




  Encapsulation
  _name convention; @property
  private / protected + properties with get/set




  MRO
  Method Resolution Order for multiple inheritance
  No multiple class inheritance — use interfaces; lookup is simpler





Python — class, __init__, self, inheritance, polymorphism:


1class Animal:


2    def __init__(self, name):


3        self.name = name          # self = this instance


4    def speak(self):


5        return "..."


6 


7class Dog(Animal):                # inheritance


8    def speak(self):              # override → polymorphism


9        return f"{self.name}: woof"


10 


11pet = Dog("Rex")                  # object / instance


12print(pet.speak())                # Rex: woof


13print(Dog.__mro__)                # MRO: Dog → Animal → object


C# — class, constructor, this, inheritance, override:


1class Animal


2{


3    public string Name { get; private set; }


4 


5    public Animal(string name)   // constructor (like __init__)


6    {


7        this.Name = name;        // this = current object (like self)


8    }


9 


10    public virtual string Speak()


11    {


12        return "...";


13    }


14}


15 


16class Dog : Animal               // single base class


17{


18    public Dog(string name) : base(name)


19    {


20    }


21 


22    public override string Speak()


23    {


24        return this.Name + ": woof";


25    }


26}


27 


28Animal pet = new Dog("Rex");     // object / instance


29Console.WriteLine(pet.Speak());  // Rex: woof


30// No MRO list — one base class (+ interfaces if needed)




Python — encapsulation (convention + property):


1class BankAccount:


2    def __init__(self, balance):


3        self._balance = balance   # _ = "internal" by convention


4 


5    @property


6    def balance(self):


7        return self._balance


C# — encapsulation (access modifiers + property):


1class BankAccount


2{


3    private decimal _balance;    // truly private


4 


5    public BankAccount(decimal balance)


6    {


7        this._balance = balance;


8    }


9 


10    public decimal Balance


11    {


12        get { return this._balance; }   // read-only property


13    }


14}




Bottom line: Same OOP ideas in both languages. Biggest gaps: Python self is explicit; C# this is implicit. Python allows multiple inheritance + MRO; C# uses one base class + interfaces. Python privacy is mostly convention (_); C# enforces private.






  
  
  
  
  Navigation
